failure_patterns.pattern: Treating 'international student' as the differentiator rather than what was built during the experience
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students conflate the credential (the label '留学生') with actual competitive advantage, and don't build the language, cultural, or network capital that would make the experience genuinely valuable to employers
failure_patterns.consequence: Return to China without any concrete differentiator, discover the label alone has little value, experience sharp psychological disillusionment
warning_signs: Can't name specific companies that would value your regional experience
Primary social circle abroad was entirely other Chinese students
Spent majority of free time consuming Chinese-language media and maintaining China-based relationships
failure_patterns._source: zhihu_出国留学后应不应该回国.txt

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating H-1B as a near-certainty and making life plans that depend on it
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Availability bias — people in CS hear success stories constantly and underweight the real lottery probability, especially in non-STEM fields where only one attempt is possible
failure_patterns.consequence: Sample 4: three failed H-1B draws forced relocation to Canada; Sample 8: OPT layoff during 60-day window forced return to China; both lost years of career positioning
warning_signs: Making housing, relationship, or financial commitments that require staying in the US before H-1B is confirmed
Not having a Canada/Europe/return-to-home-country contingency plan during OPT
failure_patterns._source: zhihu_如果你已经有了美国工作签_你会选择留美还是回国.txt

failure_patterns.pattern: Returning to China without a differentiated advantage and competing directly with locals
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The cultural prestige of a 'sea turtle' returnee creates false confidence that foreign experience alone commands premium positioning
failure_patterns.consequence: Ends up earning only slightly above local average — the 'returnee premium' is small without genuine managerial or technical differentiation
warning_signs: No managerial track record from the US stint
Returning without a structured offer from a multinational
Assuming the US brand name alone will open doors
failure_patterns._source: zhihu_未来应留在美国还是回国生活.txt

failure_patterns.pattern: Perpetual deferral: saying 'I'll return in a few years' while accumulating life anchors that make return progressively harder
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Each individual life decision (buying a house, getting married, having children) feels unrelated to the return decision, but cumulatively they raise the exit cost to prohibitive levels — boiling frog dynamic
failure_patterns.consequence: People who genuinely wanted to return spend their entire career abroad not because they chose to, but because they never explicitly chose to stay — they just never chose to leave
warning_signs: You've been saying 'maybe next year' for more than 2 years
You're making large fixed purchases (property, vehicles) without having resolved the stay-vs-return question
failure_patterns._source: zhihu_海归女硕士一枚_快毕业了是继续留在美国还是回国工作.txt

failure_patterns.pattern: Anchoring the stay-vs-return decision on recent negative events rather than long-term trend
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Availability bias — high-profile incidents (e.g., Tangshan assault, Henan red-code scandal, unfinished housing) become cognitively overweighted, making recent years feel uniquely bad even when historical baseline was worse
failure_patterns.consequence: Commenter labels this 'historical amnesia syndrome' — the person misjudges the trend direction and makes a decision based on a distorted baseline
warning_signs: Citing only recent events as evidence that a country 'is declining'
Forgetting or dismissing equivalent or worse problems from prior decades

failure_patterns.pattern: Returning home without a concrete job plan, assuming overseas experience will open doors
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Availability heuristic — the person can recall stories of successful returnees and assumes the path is clear; does not account for structural barriers like local networks and high competition
failure_patterns.consequence: Extended unemployment, lower-than-expected salary offers, and difficulty re-entering host country if return fails
warning_signs: Cannot name specific companies or roles they would target upon return
Has not researched typical salary ranges or job search timelines in home city

failure_patterns.pattern: Failing to account for spouse language score in CRS projections
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates typically research their own profile factors and treat the spouse score as an afterthought or administrative detail rather than a high-value optimization lever
failure_patterns.consequence: Missing ~20 points that could have been captured with a single IELTS sitting by the spouse
warning_signs: CRS calculator filled out with spouse section left blank or estimated low
No plan for spouse to take an approved language test

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating a CRS score as a fixed asset rather than a moving target
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates calculate their CRS score once and anchor on it, not realizing draw cutoffs fluctuate based on applicant pool composition and IRCC policy
failure_patterns.consequence: People with 'safe' scores get surprised when draws don't happen or cutoffs spike; people with 'low' scores give up without exploring PNP backdoors
warning_signs: Asking 'is my 480 CRS score enough?' without specifying which draw or which stream
Not monitoring draw history trends over 6-12 months

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating immigration wait periods as requiring constant vigilance — daily or multiple-times-daily portal checking
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The illusion of control: checking feels like doing something productive during a period of genuine helplessness; anxiety seeks any available action
failure_patterns.consequence: The wait feels endless, anxiety is amplified, and the high-frequency checking adds no information since processing times don't update daily
warning_signs: Checking IRCC portal more than once per day
Feeling compelled to check after every news item about immigration draws
Describing the wait as 'endless' or 'unbearable'

failure_patterns.pattern: Submitting unofficial or informal completion documentation instead of the official registrar letter
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students receive congratulatory emails from professors or department advisors and assume these serve as official proof of program completion
failure_patterns.consequence: IRCC rejects or delays the application pending submission of proper documentation; risks missing the 180-day window if correction takes time
warning_signs: Applicant mentions using a 'program completion email' as graduation proof
Applicant has not contacted the registrar's office directly for an official letter

failure_patterns.pattern: Spending the entire job search on cold applications to large companies without pivoting to networking
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Large company brand recognition creates an anchoring bias; candidates over-invest in low-probability targets because the upside feels higher, while the structural disadvantage (application volume, no referral) is underweighted
failure_patterns.consequence: Weeks of near-zero response rate, depleting time on PGWP and eroding confidence before the higher-yield strategy (networking, referrals, mid-size companies) is attempted
warning_signs: Application list dominated by Amazon, Google, Shopify with no mid-size companies
More than 4 weeks of applications with fewer than 3 responses and no change in strategy

failure_patterns.pattern: Delaying language test preparation until after finding a job
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Job search feels more urgent and immediate; language prep feels like a background task that can wait — but CRS score timing affects when an ITA can be received
failure_patterns.consequence: Lower CRS score during the most competitive draw windows, potentially missing ITA rounds that would have been achievable with a completed TEF/TCF score
warning_signs: Starting Express Entry profile without French scores despite having French background
Waiting until after 1-year CEC eligibility to begin IELTS prep

failure_patterns.pattern: Self-eliminating from roles at companies that say 'no sponsorship' without clarifying scope
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates assume 'no sponsorship' is a binary, blanket policy covering all visa types including OPT — they do not probe whether the policy means only H-1B
failure_patterns.consequence: Missed opportunities at companies that would have hired them on OPT or even covered STEM OPT extension paperwork
warning_signs: Immediately removing a company from consideration after a 'no sponsorship' statement without follow-up questions
Never asking the recruiter to specify what 'sponsorship' means in their context

failure_patterns.pattern: Asking for a job (or interview) in the first cold email
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The sender conflates the goal of the email (get a response) with the ultimate goal (get a job), and front-loads the high-commitment ask
failure_patterns.consequence: Instant close — high-ask openers in cold email have near-zero conversion because they require the recipient to make a large decision with no prior relationship
warning_signs: Email closing asks for an interview, a job application review, or a hiring decision
Email is framed around what the sender needs rather than what value they bring

failure_patterns.pattern: Pursuing a PhD to enter software engineering, treating the degree as a general career enhancer
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The PhD signals intelligence and rigor, and students conflate the research credential with a general career premium; the SWE job market's actual indifference to PhDs for non-research roles is not visible until job searching
failure_patterns.consequence: 4-5 years of below-market stipend income with minimal salary uplift in SWE roles compared to peers who entered industry directly — compounding financial disadvantage
warning_signs: Student cannot articulate which specific role type requires a PhD
Student frames PhD as 'keeping options open' rather than targeting a specific research outcome
Student's internship experiences during PhD are all SWE, not research

failure_patterns.pattern: Confusing the OPT EAD expiration date with the I-20 program end date when calculating when the 60-day grace period begins
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Both dates appear on official documents and students anchor to whichever date is more salient (usually the EAD card they carry), without understanding which controls the grace period trigger
failure_patterns.consequence: Student miscalculates how much time they have, potentially staying in the US or attempting status transitions after their actual authorized stay has ended
warning_signs: Student quotes only their EAD expiration date when describing their timeline
Student has not cross-referenced I-20 program end date with DSO

failure_patterns.pattern: Using a general employment attorney rather than an immigration specialist for H-1B filing
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Employer's existing outside counsel handles employment matters broadly; company does not distinguish immigration specialty from general employment law
failure_patterns.consequence: Weaker specialty occupation documentation, wrong SOC code selection, higher RFE and denial rates — the poster experienced this for two years before switching firms
warning_signs: Attorney's primary practice area is listed as 'employment law' not 'immigration'
Attorney does not proactively ask about SOC code strategy or specialty occupation documentation

failure_patterns.pattern: Attempting to structure a cap-exempt dual-employment arrangement without an immigration attorney
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The strategy appears straightforward on the surface (work part-time for university, file through them); complexity of USCIS requirements and audit risk is underestimated
failure_patterns.consequence: Improperly structured arrangement fails USCIS scrutiny; in audit scenarios, serious immigration consequences including potential status violations
warning_signs: Searching for 'how to file cap-exempt H-1B myself' or similar DIY framing
Treating the arrangement as primarily a paperwork exercise rather than a genuine employment relationship

failure_patterns.pattern: Accumulating 12 or more months of full-time CPT without realizing OPT is forfeited
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The rule sounds like an exact boundary ('12 months') but is a cumulative ceiling; students who take breaks between internships and resume CPT later can cross it without a single continuous 12-month stint
failure_patterns.consequence: Permanent loss of OPT eligibility for that degree level, eliminating the post-graduation work authorization buffer required for H-1B lottery participation
warning_signs: Student has done multiple CPT internships and has not tracked cumulative months
Student believes the 12-month rule resets between employers or after a break

failure_patterns.pattern: Listing a backup country without genuinely exploring it, leaving the psychological safety valve non-functional
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: People acknowledge they 'should' have a backup but resist emotionally committing to it because doing so feels like accepting failure on the primary path
failure_patterns.consequence: The backup remains a fiction; when the primary option fails, the person is unprepared and the desperation that follows leads to rushed, poor decisions
warning_signs: Saying 'I could always go to Canada' without having researched specific programs, costs, or pathways
Never having spoken to anyone who actually made the backup move

failure_patterns.pattern: Winning H-1B lottery but losing the petition due to job title not qualifying as specialty occupation
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates conflate H-1B lottery selection with H-1B approval; companies in non-tech sectors (e.g., small supply chain/procurement firms) often cannot demonstrate that the role requires a specialized degree unavailable from US workers
failure_patterns.consequence: Forced departure despite having 'won' the lottery; loss of sunk cost in OPT period and job; forced binary choice between expensive private master's and returning
warning_signs: Job title is generic (e.g., 'procurement analyst', 'marketing coordinator') rather than technically specialized
Employer is a small firm without prior H-1B sponsorship history

failure_patterns.pattern: Directly applying for target-level roles without the matching credentials or experience
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Ambition without realistic self-assessment; the 'one bite to become fat' (一口吃成胖子) mentality
failure_patterns.consequence: Repeated rejection leads to psychological crash and self-abandonment rather than a recalibrated strategy
warning_signs: Applying only to top-tier roles with no backup plan
No awareness of stepping-stone roles in the target industry

failure_patterns.pattern: Attempting to '转码' (pivot to coding via bootcamp) without genuine interest in software engineering
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Social comparison with CS peers creates pressure to replicate their income trajectory; income becomes the goal rather than fit
failure_patterns.consequence: Sample 5 spent thousands on a bootcamp but discovered zero interest in coding, compounding his sense of failure and identity crisis
warning_signs: Deciding to learn coding primarily because peers earn more, not because of intrinsic interest
Choosing a bootcamp as a last resort during a visa crisis rather than a planned career move

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating technical skill as the primary career asset in China
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Chinese engineers in the US observe that technical depth is rewarded in US tech culture and assume the same logic applies in China's corporate environment
failure_patterns.consequence: Gets stuck at individual contributor level while less technically skilled but better politically positioned peers advance — the top answer explicitly warns that pure technical focus without business/management orientation leads to being sidelined
warning_signs: Dismissing the importance of internal visibility and business framing
No interest in moving toward team lead or project ownership roles
Belief that code quality alone drives career advancement

failure_patterns.pattern: Comparing raw salaries across countries without adjusting for local purchasing power or career trajectory
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Nominal salary numbers are concrete and easy to compare; the complexity of local cost-of-living, tax rates, career ceiling, and equity opportunity is harder to quantify
failure_patterns.consequence: Staying abroad for a salary premium that, after adjustment, may be smaller than assumed — while missing a faster-growth career trajectory at home
warning_signs: Framing the decision as 'US $250K vs. China RMB 110K' without further adjustment
Not accounting for the fact that $37K USD is a low salary in a major US city

failure_patterns.pattern: Making the stay-vs-return decision based on peer social comparison rather than personal circumstances
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Social comparison bias amplified by social media — seeing home country peers' apparent success (social events, business activity) against one's own quiet life abroad triggers FOMO-driven decisions
failure_patterns.consequence: Returning for emotional reasons into a market the person is not prepared for, or staying abroad in a state of chronic dissatisfaction
warning_signs: Frequently mentions friends back home doing well or looking successful on social media
Decision framing is about 'missing out' rather than specific opportunities

failure_patterns.pattern: Imposter syndrome causing over-compliance behavior — never complaining, never making mistakes, constant best-behavior performance
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Internalized belief that immigrant status is conditional on perfect behavior; feeling that you 'don't belong here yet' and any misstep could be disqualifying
failure_patterns.consequence: Chronic stress, inability to advocate for oneself professionally, and a distorted sense that normal workplace behavior is off-limits
warning_signs: Feeling unable to raise workplace concerns because of immigration status
Describing yourself as needing to be 'on best behavior constantly'
Feeling that normal human mistakes could threaten your right to stay

failure_patterns.pattern: Defaulting entirely to job board applications after graduation
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Job boards are the visible, socially legitimized channel; cold outreach feels uncomfortable and unfamiliar; optimism bias leads students to believe volume will eventually yield results
failure_patterns.consequence: Months pass with near-zero callback rate; OPT clock burns down; students interpret the failure as a skills problem rather than a channel problem
warning_signs: Student has applied to 100+ jobs through portals with fewer than 5 callbacks
Student attributes all rejections to skills gaps or resume quality without testing alternative channels

failure_patterns.pattern: Conflating program prestige with placement quality for industry research roles
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Program rankings are heavily publicized and socially salient; the advisor-level industry network variable is granular and requires active due diligence to uncover
failure_patterns.consequence: Students choose rank-5 programs with no industry-connected advisors over rank-20 programs with direct pipelines to top AI labs, resulting in worse industry research placement
warning_signs: Student primarily references US News rankings when evaluating PhD programs for industry track
Student has not researched individual advisor placement records
Student assumes top program automatically means better industry access

failure_patterns.pattern: Failing to ask employer about cap-exempt bridge options until status is already in jeopardy
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Workers assume cap-exempt sponsorship is only available at universities and do not know that some employers have affiliated cap-exempt entities
failure_patterns.consequence: Missing a viable path that could have been arranged proactively, forcing reactive decisions during the 60-day grace period
warning_signs: Employee has never asked HR about affiliated nonprofit or university partnerships
Employee is approaching second or third OPT year with no backup status plan

failure_patterns.pattern: Choosing an internship target without verifying H-1B sponsorship history
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students optimize for brand name, compensation, or role quality without treating visa sponsorship as a hard filter
failure_patterns.consequence: Return offer accepted, then company declines to sponsor H-1B — student must restart job search during OPT, now under time pressure
warning_signs: Student has not looked up the company on H1Bdata.info or MyVisaJobs before accepting
Company is a startup or small firm with no prior international hiring history

failure_patterns.pattern: Optimizing for career excitement and 'changing the world' over financial stability, then discovering the Chinese job market is equally or more competitive
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Availability bias and youthful ambition cause the person to romanticize the dynamism of China's economy while underweighting the concrete financial and lifestyle advantages already in hand in the US
failure_patterns.consequence: Sacrificed 3+ years of US earning compounding and international experience for a Chinese job market grind that was not meaningfully more exciting or rewarding
warning_signs: Framing the US job as 'just going through the motions' or 'quasi-retirement' without concrete evidence of a better opportunity in China
Returning without a specific job offer or sector in China secured in advance
failure_patterns._source: zhihu_出国留学后到底是否回国工作.txt

failure_patterns.pattern: Staying in a miserable situation because of sunk cost in the immigration process
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Years of OPT applications, H-1B filings, and green card waiting create a psychological investment that makes leaving feel like 'wasting' everything
failure_patterns.consequence: Multiple samples describe multi-year unhappiness in situations they couldn't exit because doing so felt like surrendering the investment
warning_signs: Framing the decision as 'I can't leave after everything I've put in'
Staying in a country or job you actively dislike primarily to protect immigration status
failure_patterns._source: zhihu_如果你已经有了美国工作签_你会选择留美还是回国.txt

failure_patterns.pattern: Staying indefinitely in a mismatched career due to visa dependency
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Sunk cost and status quo bias — having invested years obtaining the H-1B and working toward green card, the psychological cost of abandoning the path feels enormous
failure_patterns.consequence: Spends the majority of working life in a role that produces no internal satisfaction, with the implicit comfort that 'I could have done more if I'd gone back' remaining permanently unresolved
warning_signs: Counting down to 5pm daily
Justifying continued stay with external reasons only (green card, stability, salary) with no positive internal motivations
Frequent fantasy about alternative paths not taken
failure_patterns._source: zhihu_未来应留在美国还是回国生活.txt

failure_patterns.pattern: Letting immigration status anxiety drive major career and life decisions
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: OPT and H-1B create real uncertainty, and the emotional weight of 'will I get to stay' can cause people to optimize for visa preservation rather than career quality
failure_patterns.consequence: Taking inferior jobs that offer sponsorship, staying in roles with no growth because switching is risky, and experiencing chronic low-grade anxiety that distorts all other decisions
warning_signs: Describing your job situation as '寄人篱下' (living under someone else's roof / dependent status)
Evaluating job offers primarily on visa sponsorship rather than role quality
failure_patterns._source: zhihu_海归女硕士一枚_快毕业了是继续留在美国还是回国工作.txt

failure_patterns.pattern: Emailing HR instead of the hiring manager for cold outreach
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: HR contact information is more visible and feels like the 'correct' channel; students conflate the formal application process with cold outreach
failure_patterns.consequence: Emails are filtered or ignored at the screening layer; sponsorship flags are applied before any personal evaluation occurs
warning_signs: Outreach target has 'HR', 'Talent Acquisition', or 'Recruiter' in their title
Student is choosing contacts based on visibility rather than hiring authority

failure_patterns.pattern: Partners having fundamentally incompatible visions for which country to live in, discovered only after marriage
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The topic is emotionally charged and couples avoid direct confrontation during dating; political/cultural worldview differences are minimized until they become structurally forced
failure_patterns.consequence: Sample 7: husband pressured wife to return to China for years, relationship eventually broke down and ended in divorce after she got her green card
warning_signs: Partner consistently framing the home country as superior without genuine discussion
Relying on H-4 EAD as the immigration plan for one partner — creates structural dependency and resentment

failure_patterns.pattern: Over-investing in networking activities before establishing core competence
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: MBA culture and career advice strongly emphasize networking as a primary career lever — this feels actionable and social, unlike the slow grind of skill-building
failure_patterns.consequence: Collects contacts and business cards but has no real value to offer, resulting in no material career benefit from the networking investment
warning_signs: Attending multiple networking events per week while feeling career is stagnant
Measuring networking success by volume of contacts rather than quality of exchanges
Startup founder attending pitch events before product-market fit exists

failure_patterns.pattern: Returning to China after extended US stay and expecting smooth reintegration
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: People project their memories of home onto the current reality; they underestimate how much both they and the country have changed
failure_patterns.consequence: Sample 8 and Sample 12 both experienced significant unhappiness after return — Sample 8 is now attempting to re-emigrate to Canada; Sample 12 described the return as 'rebirth' but this was unique to his particular alienation in the US
warning_signs: Making return decision primarily to escape US problems rather than genuinely wanting China's environment
Returning during or immediately after a period of personal crisis (layoff, breakup, depression)

diagnostic_questions.question: Does the candidate have Canadian work experience, and if so, how many years?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines eligibility for the Canadian Experience Class (CEC) stream and the number of CRS points earned from Canadian work experience (up to 5 years)
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Confirm the NOC code of the Canadian work experience to assess CEC eligibility and category-based draw eligibility
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Candidate may need to rely on FSWP or FSTP; CEC pathway is unavailable

diagnostic_questions.question: What is the worker's country of birth, and is it India or China?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines which EB per-country backlog applies; Indian nationals face an approximately 175-year EB-2 backlog while Chinese nationals face a qualitatively different 5–10 year EB-2 wait
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If India: evaluate whether indefinite H-1B renewal is the realistic trajectory; assess AC21 portability and priority date preservation as core risk management tools
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If China or other country: apply country-specific backlog data; Chinese nationals have a materially different stay-or-return calculus than Indian nationals

diagnostic_questions.question: What is the candidate's current CRS score, and does it meet the threshold for general draws (500+) or STEM category draws (470–510)?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines whether the candidate is currently competitive for an ITA without a PNP nomination
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Candidate may be competitive in the next general or category-based draw; monitor draw frequency and cutoffs
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Candidate should assess PNP eligibility to add +600 points or identify category-based draws with lower cutoffs

diagnostic_questions.question: Has the worker's I-140 been approved, and has the priority date been in queue for at least 180 days?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines AC21 portability eligibility for job changes without losing green card queue position
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Worker may change employers if new role is in same or similar occupational classification; priority date is preserved
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If I-140 not yet approved or 180-day threshold not met: employer change carries risk of losing priority date position; worker should evaluate timing carefully

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the candidate eligible for a Provincial Nominee Program (PNP) stream, particularly the BC PNP Tech stream?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: PNP nomination adds +600 CRS points, which is the most decisive single factor in achieving Express Entry selection
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Pursue PNP nomination immediately; BC PNP Tech can nominate within 2 business days for in-demand tech NOC codes
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Assess other provincial streams (OINP, AAIP, MPNP) or focus on improving raw CRS score

diagnostic_questions.question: What DOL wage level (I–IV) is assigned to the worker's current H-1B position?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines lottery entry weighting under the wage-weighted lottery system effective February 27, 2026; Level IV workers receive 4 entries vs. Level I's 1 entry
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If Level IV: worker has disproportionate lottery advantage under new rules; this is a significant factor in cap-subject petition strategy
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If Level I or II: worker is in the majority (Level II = 36% of FY2023 approvals) but has reduced relative lottery probability under new wage-weighted system; consider whether wage renegotiation or employer change could elevate level

diagnostic_questions.question: Does the candidate's NOC code fall under STEM occupation categories targeted by IRCC category-based draws (e.g., NOC 20012, 21231, 21232)?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines eligibility for STEM category-based draws, which have lower CRS cutoffs (481–510) than general draws
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Candidate should ensure profile is flagged for STEM category draws; lower cutoff may allow ITA without PNP
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Candidate must rely on general draws or other category draws (healthcare, trades, transport, French language)

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the worker employed by a cap-exempt institution (university, nonprofit research organization)?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines whether annual cap lottery applies; cap-exempt employers filed 39,700 approvals in FY2023 outside the 85,000-slot cap
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Worker is insulated from cap lottery uncertainty; H-1B petition proceeds directly to adjudication
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Worker is subject to cap lottery with approximately 22–28% annual approval probability; lottery timing and wage level classification become critical planning variables

diagnostic_questions.question: Does the candidate have strong French language skills above CLB 7 in all four language areas?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines eligibility for +50 additional CRS points and access to French language proficiency draws with significantly lower CRS cutoffs (400–450 range)
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Submit TEF/TCF scores; claim +50 CRS points and assess eligibility for French language draw pathway
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: French language draw pathway and +50 points are unavailable; focus on other CRS improvement strategies

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the worker's occupation classified under a computer-related SOC code (SOC 15-xxxx) or a management code (SOC 11-xxxx)?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines applicable prevailing wage benchmark and median wage comparison; computer occupations median is $124,000; Computer and Information Systems Managers median is $155,700 in FY2023
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If computer-related: worker is in the 65.1% majority of H-1B approvals; benchmark wages are well-established
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If management or other category: applies different wage benchmarks and specialty occupation criteria; product managers specifically file under SOC 11-3021 or 11-2021

diagnostic_questions.question: How old is the candidate, and are they approaching or past age 45?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Age is a core CRS human capital factor; significant point decline after 45 reduces competitiveness and creates time pressure to apply
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Urgency to apply increases; delay compounds CRS score loss from age factor
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Candidate retains full age-based CRS points; less urgency from age factor alone

diagnostic_questions.question: Does the candidate have a sibling who is a Canadian citizen or PR holder?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Sibling status adds +15 additional CRS points
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Claim +15 additional CRS points in Express Entry profile
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: No additional points available from this factor

diagnostic_questions.question: Does the candidate have any criminal record or history of visa violations or immigration misrepresentation?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Inadmissibility issues can extend processing times significantly beyond the 6-month service standard and may result in a denial
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Seek legal assessment of admissibility before submitting Express Entry profile; prepare for extended processing
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Standard processing timelines apply; no additional inadmissibility risk

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the candidate an Indian national currently on US H-1B status?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Reveals comparative immigration security context: Indian nationals face a ~134-year EB-2 backlog in the US vs. ~1–2 year Canadian PR timeline — a fundamentally different stay-or-return calculus
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Canadian Express Entry PR (~1–2 years) represents resolved immigration status vs. indefinite H-1B dependency; this changes the financial and personal planning calculus significantly
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Assess nationality-specific US backlog (e.g., EB-2 China: 5–10 years) to determine comparative urgency of Canadian PR pathway

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your current I-140 category and country of chargeability?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines whether you face a 1–5 year wait (most nationalities, EB-1A) or a 40–134 year structural trap (Indian national EB-2/EB-3) — the entire decision framework changes based on this answer
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If Indian national on EB-2/EB-3: What is your priority date and how does it compare to current Visa Bulletin cut-offs?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If not Indian or Chinese: What is your current priority date gap and how many years realistically remain?

diagnostic_questions.question: How many of the last 15 years have you held green card status?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether exit tax analysis is required at all; the 8-of-15-year threshold is the gateway to covered expatriate status
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If 8 or more: What is your current estimated net worth including all worldwide assets at fair market value, and what was your average annual US tax liability for the last 5 years?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If fewer than 8: Exit tax risk is zero; shift focus to 401k distribution strategy, FBAR compliance history, and green card abandonment timing

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your current RRSP balance, and do you know your home country's non-resident withholding rate under the Canada tax treaty?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines the actual after-tax value of your RRSP as a non-resident and whether pre-departure withdrawal strategies should be pursued
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Model the partial-year marginal rate scenario: is your effective rate in the departure year lower than 25%? If so, quantify how much to withdraw before leaving.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Look up the Canada tax treaty with your home country specifically for the pension/RRSP article — do not assume any reduction exists; India and China receive no reduction from the default 25%

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you ever had a formal assessment of your EB-1A eligibility from an immigration attorney?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Reveals whether the person has explored the primary escape hatch from the EB-2/EB-3 trap; most people who would qualify have never been told they might
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What criteria did the attorney assess, and what was the outcome? When was this assessment done relative to your current career stage?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: What is your current publication record, salary percentile relative to peers, awards, media coverage, or roles judging others' work? These are the EB-1A evidentiary pillars.

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you formally abandoned your green card via Form I-407, or are you still technically a lawful permanent resident?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person is currently accruing US tax residency obligations on worldwide income without realizing it
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If abandoned: Confirm residency termination date and whether Form 8854 was filed if required; verify final year FBAR was filed
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If not abandoned: Calculate how long they've been living abroad as an undeclared US tax resident and assess FBAR exposure for unreported foreign accounts

diagnostic_questions.question: Are you planning to sell your Canadian property before or after you leave, and do you know what Section 116 withholding means for your cash flow?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Reveals whether the person has modeled the gross-price withholding versus the gain-based tax bill, and whether they have budgeted for months of illiquidity
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Ask for their timeline: when do they need the proceeds? If within 6 months of closing, the clearance certificate delay could be a serious problem.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Walk through the mechanics: 25% of gross sale price is withheld by the buyer, not 25% of gain — on an $800K property, that is $200K held up regardless of actual tax owed

diagnostic_questions.question: Does your spouse work in the US, and if so, under what visa status?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: If the spouse is on H-4 EAD, the household has a hidden single point of failure — the principal applicant's employment continuity determines both people's work authorization simultaneously
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Is the H-4 EAD dependent on an approved I-140? What is the household's financial plan if the primary applicant faces a 60-day grace period clock?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Does the spouse have independent immigration status, or are they currently unable to work? This affects the financial calculus of staying vs. returning significantly.

diagnostic_questions.question: Are you returning to India or China, and how long have you been physically present in your home country in the current tax year?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Which home-country tax residency rules apply and whether the RNOR window is available (India only) or whether stricter 183-day worldwide income taxation applies (China)
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If India and within first 2 years: Model large US retirement distributions during RNOR period to avoid Indian taxation on those withdrawals
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If China or past RNOR window: Assess current double-taxation exposure and treaty claims available under US-China or post-RNOR US-India treaty provisions

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you severed — or do you plan to sever — all primary Canadian residential ties before your intended departure date?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Identifies whether the person is at risk of being classified as a continuing Canadian tax resident despite physically living abroad
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Ask specifically about the home (sold or lease terminated?), spouse and dependents (relocating with you?), and provincial health card (cancelled?).
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Explain the 'extended stay overseas' trap: CRA does not automatically reclassify you as a non-resident; maintaining a home or spouse in Canada is sufficient to sustain Canadian tax residency

diagnostic_questions.question: What major life decisions have you deferred because you are waiting for your green card?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Surfaces the hidden cost of the wait — if someone has deferred homeownership, children, eldercare for parents, or career moves for 5+ years, they are already paying the 'immigration tax' whether they name it or not
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: How long have these decisions been deferred? What is the compounding cost of continued deferral if the wait extends another 10–20 years?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Have you fully internalized that EB-2/EB-3 India timelines are 50–134 years under current policy, or are you operating on an assumption of resolution within 10–15 years?

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you own US real estate, and if so, have you decided whether to sell before or after your departure?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether FIRPTA withholding will apply to a future sale and whether the 15% gross proceeds withholding creates a liquidity or planning problem
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If planning to sell after departure: Have you modeled the FIRPTA withholding impact on cash flow at closing and the filing requirements to recover any overpayment?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If selling before departure: Confirm residency status at time of sale to ensure non-resident rules don't apply prematurely

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your planned departure date, and have you modeled your total Canadian income for that partial calendar year?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Reveals whether there is a planning window to make RRSP withdrawals or realize non-registered gains at a lower marginal rate before departure
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Run the numbers: what is the effective marginal rate on incremental income in that partial year? Compare to the flat 25% RRSP withholding rate post-departure.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The departure date is one of the most important tax planning variables — even a few months of difference changes whether pre-departure RRSP withdrawal is advantageous

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have or could you access $800K–$1.05M for an EB-5 investment?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines whether the fastest current no-backlog green card path is available; for high-earning professionals or those with family capital, this may be a live option that has never been seriously evaluated
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Have you consulted with an EB-5 attorney about rural or TEA project timelines (4–12 months processing)? How does that compare to your EB-2/EB-3 wait?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: At your current savings rate and compensation trajectory, when would this capital threshold become accessible? Is that timeline competitive with other options?

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you filed FBARs for every year you held foreign financial accounts exceeding $10,000 while you were a US person?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person has prior FBAR exposure that requires voluntary disclosure before departure, and the magnitude of potential penalty liability
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If fully compliant: No remediation needed; confirm FBAR obligation ends after final departure year filing
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If gaps exist: Assess whether violations were non-willful ($10,000/year penalty) or willful (50% of account balance/year); consider IRS Streamlined Filing Compliance Procedures before departing

diagnostic_questions.question: Did you use the RRSP Home Buyers' Plan or Lifelong Learning Plan, and do you know your outstanding repayment balance?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Identifies a silent ongoing obligation that continues post-departure and can generate unexpected Canadian taxable income if ignored
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Calculate the annual repayment amount and decide whether to repay the full balance before departure (using current marginal rate) or accept the annual income inclusion going forward.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Check CRA My Account for HBP/LLP balances before finalizing departure plans — this is frequently overlooked and creates avoidable tax exposure

diagnostic_questions.question: When did you last check the Visa Bulletin, and do you know whether annual EB-3 visas were exhausted before fiscal year end in the last two years?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Tests whether the person understands that annual cap exhaustion is a recurring structural problem — not just queue position — that makes practical filing impossible even when priority dates appear current
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If aware of exhaustion: How have you adjusted your planning to account for the gap between apparent priority date currency and actual ability to file?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: This is a critical gap in understanding your actual timeline — the EB-3/EW cap was exhausted by September 9, 2025 for FY2025 and August 16, 2024 for FY2024.

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your plan for your 401k or IRA — leave in place, roll over, or withdraw?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person is about to make the most common costly mistake (early withdrawal) or has thought through the tax-deferred compounding and treaty-based distribution strategy
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If planning early withdrawal: Are you under 59½? Have you calculated the after-tax value including 10% penalty, ordinary income tax, and state tax versus leaving funds to grow?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If leaving in place: Have you filed Form W-8BEN with your custodian to claim treaty-reduced withholding rates on future distributions?

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have a non-registered investment portfolio in Canada, and have you calculated your adjusted cost base on those holdings?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines the size of the deemed disposition tax hit on departure and whether pre-departure realization of gains (when Canadian marginal rates may be lower) is preferable to the deemed disposition
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Compare tax cost of realizing gains before departure at partial-year marginal rate versus deemed disposition at the same rate — they may be equivalent, but timing of actual cash payment differs.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Many investors do not track ACB carefully; without it, calculating the departure tax obligation is impossible and CRA may use a conservative (unfavorable) estimate

diagnostic_questions.question: Are you tracking any specific immigration legislation, and has an anticipated bill affected any decision you have made in the last two years?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Identifies whether the person is making real decisions based on low-probability legislative outcomes — a major failure pattern that can defer action for years
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What is your assessment of the historical passage rate of similar bills? What is your contingency plan if the bill does not pass in the next two years?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Good — are you aware that visa recapture and country-neutral proposals have been debated for over a decade without enactment?

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your current immigration status in Canada — PGWP, PR application in process, or confirmed PR?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines whether visa precarity is still a live variable in the decision; PGWP holders face real uncertainty that PR holders do not, which changes the urgency and risk profile of the decision
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If PR confirmed: have you calculated your 730-day compliance for the current 5-year window, and how much margin do you have?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If still on PGWP: what is your timeline to PR eligibility, and is your current employer sponsoring or are you applying independently via Express Entry?

diagnostic_questions.question: Is your household single-income or dual-income, and have you modeled what dual income would add to your annual savings?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the current savings shortfall is structural (single income in high-cost city) or whether an obvious lever has not been pulled
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What is the delta between single and dual income scenarios in your model — does dual income push you above the CAD $25,000/year savings threshold?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Run the dual-income model before drawing any conclusions about whether Canada is financially viable for your household

diagnostic_questions.question: How old are your children, and how long have they been in the US school system?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Places the children in the risk framework — under 5 (low disruption), 8–14 (high risk), late high school (manageable); also reveals depth of US educational identity formed
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If children are 8–14: What is your specific plan for school continuity in the destination city, and have you visited those schools?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If children are under 5: Have you mapped out the schooling path from primary through university in the destination city given their legal status?

diagnostic_questions.question: What does your partner actually want to do with their career, in their own terms — not whether they're supportive of your decision?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether stated support reflects genuine preference alignment or conflict avoidance; unresolved misalignment surfaces post-relocation when reversal is costly
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If they have a clear preference: does that preference have a viable path in the destination you're considering, independently of your situation?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If they haven't articulated a clear preference: this is a red flag — the decision is being made without their career interests being modeled at all

diagnostic_questions.question: How old are your parents, and what is their current health status?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether eldercare is an immediate active need, a plannable near-term need, or a longer-horizon concern — the answer determines urgency and appropriate response
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If parents are 75+ or have a diagnosed condition: What specific care tasks are currently unmet, and who is currently providing what support?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If parents are 60–68 and healthy: Have you mapped what your response would be if their health declines in the next 5 years, and does your current career plan accommodate that?

diagnostic_questions.question: When was your last extended visit home, how long was it, and how did it feel by week 3?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Week 3 strips away honeymoon effect and reveals the underlying friction between the person's reshaped identity and home-country environment — the most reliable proxy for what sustained return will feel like
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What specifically felt off by week 3 — social dynamics, pace, communication norms, infrastructure? That's likely what will compound over months 6–12
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If you haven't had a recent extended visit, you are making the return decision on outdated and likely idealized information — a 3–4 week trip before deciding is essential

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your actual annual liquid savings number — after all taxes, rent, healthcare, and immigration fees?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person has run a real deduction model or is reasoning from gross salary; reveals actual financial accumulation rate
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What percentage of gross is that, and have you included immigration legal fees as a recurring line item?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Walk through the deduction template together before making any financial comparison to a home-country scenario

diagnostic_questions.question: Is your profession subject to country-specific licensing requirements?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the return is to the same professional role or to a fundamentally different one — medicine and law face hard barriers; tech and finance do not
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What is the exact re-qualification pathway, how long does it take, is the exam conducted in your home language, and what is the pass rate for returnees?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Does your US credential and experience carry a genuine premium in your target sector, or is it neutral to slightly positive?

diagnostic_questions.question: Can you name 3–5 specific people in your target home city who know your work quality and could hire or refer you today?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether network credentialing has been done — the most commonly neglected milestone that determines transition speed and quality
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Have any of these relationships progressed to a concrete conversation about a role or engagement in the past 12 months?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: What specific mechanisms are you using to build these relationships before departure — advising, conferences, consulting, LinkedIn?

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you built a 10-year compounding model on both paths, or are you comparing today's quality of life?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person is doing genuine analysis or rationalizing a fear-driven default; most people have not built any model
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Walk me through the model — what did you use for career ceiling, savings rate, and immigration probability? What were the key assumptions?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: What would need to be true about the home-market trajectory for return to be the better compounding path? Have you ever asked that question seriously?

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your actual monthly savings rate in the US after taxes, rent, and cost of living — and what would it be in your home city?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the US salary advantage survives cost-of-living and tax adjustment; the most common analysis failure is comparing gross salaries rather than savings rates
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If savings rate is higher in the US, model whether the gap is large enough to justify immigration tax and opportunity costs
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If savings rate is comparable or higher at home, the US financial case collapses and the decision becomes about career ceiling and lifestyle

diagnostic_questions.question: What is the current priority date for your specific visa category and country of birth, and at the current movement rate, when would you realistically receive a green card?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the green card plan is a realistic near-term goal or a 50-100+ year commitment that should not anchor career decisions
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If the wait is under 10 years: what would you do differently in those 10 years knowing this timeline? If over 10 years: what alternative pathways are you planning around instead?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Have you looked this up? If not, your entire career plan may be built on an assumption about a system you have not actually researched.

diagnostic_questions.question: Are you comparing Canada to the US, or Canada to returning home — have you separated these into two distinct decisions?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines whether the person has correctly scoped their decision; conflating these two comparisons leads to missing the US option entirely or framing a salary dissatisfaction as a return-home question
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If they've separated them: which comparison are you actually making, and what is the specific US alternative you've modeled?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If they haven't separated them: walk through the Canada-vs-US income model first before evaluating Canada-vs-home-country

diagnostic_questions.question: What city and neighborhood are you renting in, and have you compared that cost to suburban alternatives within commuting distance?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether housing — the highest-impact savings variable — has been optimized or whether the professional is paying a lifestyle premium that is eroding their financial case for staying
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What is the monthly rent delta between your current location and a comparable suburban option, and have you multiplied that by 12 to see the annual savings impact?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Calculate the Toronto core vs. Mississauga/Brampton or Vancouver core vs. Burnaby/Surrey difference — it typically represents $7,200–$10,800/year in savings

diagnostic_questions.question: What language do your children primarily think and dream in?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Reveals the depth of US cultural and linguistic identity already formed; a child dreaming in English will face a fundamentally different adaptation challenge than one who is still bilingual
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If primarily English: Have you assessed whether there are sufficient English-medium or international school options in your destination city?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If still bilingual: What has maintained the home-language fluency, and will that support structure exist in the destination?

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your partner's realistic career trajectory if you return — job market depth in their field, credential transferability, expected time to employment?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether return economics actually work for the household or only for the primary earner; identifies whether the trailing partner faces career interruption or relinquishment
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If there is a viable path: what is the realistic income gap duration, and who finances the household during that period?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If there is no viable path: the return decision requires either the partner accepting career relinquishment or the couple evaluating third-country alternatives

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have siblings in your home country, and what is their relationship to your parents?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether you are the sole potential caregiver or whether care responsibility can be shared, which is the single largest structural factor in whether return is necessary versus optional
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If siblings are present: Have you had an explicit conversation with them about how care responsibility would be divided, and what role financial support from you would play?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If you are an only child: Have you built your career and financial timeline around the assumption that return is likely within a defined horizon?

diagnostic_questions.question: What do you miss most about living in the US — and can you get that at home?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Surfaces the specific elements of abroad life that have become load-bearing for the person's wellbeing, identity, or professional functioning — and whether those are portable
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If those elements are available at home, assess whether they're actually equivalent or just superficially similar
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If those elements are not available at home, the person needs to either recalibrate expectations or identify a substitution strategy before returning

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have children, and if so, are they school-age?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether international school fees need to be modeled in the home-country scenario, which can eliminate the savings advantage of returning
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: How many children, and have you priced international school fees in the specific city you would return to?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Do you plan to have children within the 5-year horizon of this decision, and if so, in which country?

diagnostic_questions.question: Is your target employer private-market or state-owned / government-affiliated?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the returnee premium and career ceiling assumptions that apply to private-sector roles also apply to your specific opportunity — they often do not in state institutions
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Has the state institution historically promoted returnees to senior leadership, or does that tier tend to go to domestic-track candidates?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Is the private employer in a sector that has faced or is at risk of regulatory restriction in your target country?

diagnostic_questions.question: What are your exact return conditions, and have any of them shifted in the past 2 years?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person has binding pre-committed milestones or shifting placeholders; past shifts are the strongest predictor of future shifts
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What caused the shift, and what mechanism will prevent the new conditions from shifting again?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Are the conditions specific and measurable (title, dollar amount, named contacts, specific role) or vague ('when things settle down', 'after a few more years')?

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your realistic, probability-weighted path to permanent residence, and what is the median timeline?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person has a concrete plan or a vague hope; nationalities with 20+ year backlogs who treat the green card as a near-term milestone are making decisions on false premises
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What is your contingency if that path fails or the policy changes? Have you evaluated alternative paths (EB-1A, O-1, Canada, third country)?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Are you making a long-term life decision without knowing the probability that the foundational assumption (permanent status) actually materializes?

diagnostic_questions.question: What is the total legal cost you have paid or will pay for your full immigration process, and have you subtracted this from your US compensation?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person has accounted for the $20k–$100k immigration tax that is invisible in salary comparisons
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If they have modeled it, ask whether they've also quantified the time and opportunity costs of visa constraints
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If they haven't, this is a significant blind spot — walk through the full immigration cost stack before proceeding with any financial comparison

diagnostic_questions.question: Is entrepreneurship part of your 5-10 year plan?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the US visa system structurally blocks your most important career goal, making return or third-country options disproportionately valuable
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What is the specific legal pathway available to you for founding on your current visa status — have you mapped O-1, EB-1A, or NIW requirements against your current credentials?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Is this because entrepreneurship genuinely doesn't interest you, or because you have adapted your goals to fit your visa constraints without realizing it?

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your actual monthly savings rate in CAD, and what would it be if you returned home (in PPP-adjusted terms)?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Tests whether the person has done the actual financial math or is operating on impressions; reveals whether the financial case for staying is as strong as assumed
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If they've modeled it: what is the delta, and have you accounted for Toronto housing costs, childcare subsidies, and tax rates?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If they haven't modeled it: walk through the Toronto expense model and compare against a specific home-city scenario before treating finances as a known variable

diagnostic_questions.question: Are you comparing your Canadian savings to your home-country alternative using PPP-adjusted figures or market exchange rates?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the financial comparison is methodologically valid — market exchange rates systematically overstate Canada's financial advantage for Indian tech professionals
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What PPP conversion factor are you using, and does the comparison account for actual expenses in the home-country city, not just gross salary?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The comparison is likely invalid — a Bangalore senior engineer saving ₹15L–₹25L/year is PPP-comparable to a Toronto dual-income family saving CAD $41,000/year

diagnostic_questions.question: What is the all-in cost of schooling for your children in the destination city, and have you factored that into your savings-rate comparison?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines whether the financial model for returning is realistic or based on an implicit assumption of free or low-cost public schooling that may not be available to the child
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If costs have been factored in: Does the financial case for returning still hold with $15,000–$50,000 per child per year added?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If costs have not been factored in: The financial model needs to be rebuilt before a decision is made

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your partner's immigration and work authorization status in the destination country if they are not a national there?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the partner's right to reside and right to work are actually secured, or whether work authorization requires separate employer sponsorship that is not guaranteed
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If work authorization is secured or automatic: assess job market viability independently
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If work authorization is not automatic: evaluate whether third-country options (Singapore, Canada) resolve the structural problem more cleanly

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you actually talked to your parents about what they need and want from you specifically?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the return pressure is driven by a genuine expressed parental need or by the professional's internalized obligation and anticipatory anxiety
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If yes: What did they say, and does their stated preference match the decision you are currently leaning toward?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If no: Why not — and what would change about your current decision if they said 'don't return on our account'?

diagnostic_questions.question: What do your close friends back home have in common with you now — and do those friendships still feel alive?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Reveals whether the social infrastructure that would buffer repatriation distress actually exists, or whether the person is planning to return to a social life that has diverged significantly
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If friendships feel alive, probe whether that's based on recent in-person time or remote contact — the two are not equivalent indicators
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If friendships feel distant, the person needs a specific plan for building new social infrastructure before or immediately after return

diagnostic_questions.question: Which US state are you in, or would you be in?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: State income tax rate, which ranges from 0% to 13.3% and can shift the net savings comparison by $15K–$25K annually at high incomes
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Are you in California or New York? If so, the combined federal and state tax burden makes the US savings rate significantly lower than the gross suggests.
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If Texas or Florida, the no-state-income-tax advantage materially improves the US scenario and should be explicitly modeled

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your actual net savings rate in the US versus what it would be in your home country at the target role?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the income compression is as severe as the gross salary comparison suggests, or whether cost of living and tax differences close the gap significantly
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If net savings are comparable or higher at home, what non-financial factors are driving the preference to stay in the US?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Is the net savings gap large enough to be a definitive factor, or is it within the range that personal and family considerations could reasonably override?

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have a specific role, offer, or founding plan identified in the home country — not a general intention to search after arrival?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person is planning to return to start or return to search — the single biggest determinant of transition success
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Is this offer in hand, or is it a conversation in progress? Have you negotiated a start date that allows your US equity to vest?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: What is the timeline for developing a specific role pipeline before departure, and are you interviewing for home-country roles while still employed?

diagnostic_questions.question: What specific career milestone at home would you need to see to consider returning successful — and is that achievable within 5 years?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person has a concrete picture of what success-at-home looks like, or whether 'returning is failure' is an undefined feeling rather than a reasoned assessment
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Is that milestone genuinely tied to staying abroad, or is it achievable with the credentials you already have?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If you cannot define what home-market success looks like, how are you concluding that staying abroad is better?

diagnostic_questions.question: What is your realistic priority date and current USCIS cutoff for your green card category, and what does that imply about your wait time?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person understands their actual timeline to permanent status, which determines the duration of immigration tax exposure
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If wait time is 20+ years, this is a structural constraint that should reframe the entire decision — explore National Interest Waiver, O-1, or EB-1A paths
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If they don't know, they are making a major life decision without a key variable — get this information before any other analysis

diagnostic_questions.question: When you imagine returning home, what year's version of your home country are you picturing?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person is comparing current host-country life to an outdated mental model of home, systematically undervaluing the return option
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If they picture current conditions: have they looked at VC rankings, startup ecosystems, and government investment data for their specific sector in the past 12 months?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If they are uncertain: what would it take to update their mental model — what data would they look at?

diagnostic_questions.question: Is your partner able to work freely in Canada, and what would happen to their employment in each scenario?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Surfaces whether household income is being correctly modeled; partner's work authorization in Canada vs. the US vs. home country is often the decisive variable that gets overlooked in individual income comparisons
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If partner works freely in Canada: what is the household income, and how does that change the Canada-vs-US savings comparison?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If partner cannot work or is not working: is that a visa constraint or a preference, and how does it affect the household financial model?

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have Canadian PR, and has the savings model you're using accounted for the financial and psychological value of immigration security?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the professional is rationally pricing PR as a benefit or using it as an emotional anchor that is preventing honest financial analysis
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Can you articulate what that security is worth to you in dollar terms, and does staying in Canada at your current savings rate justify that cost?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The immigration uncertainty itself has a real cost — job lock, visa anxiety, restricted negotiating leverage — that should be added to the cost side of staying in Canada

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you researched the specific legal status your child will hold in the destination country and what that means for school enrollment and university admissions?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Reveals whether the parent understands the practical consequences of dual nationality non-recognition (China) or OCI status (India) for the child's educational pathway
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If yes: Have you verified this with the specific schools and universities you're targeting, not just general policy?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If no: This is a critical gap — the child's admission track and fee structure at elite universities may be significantly less favorable than the parent assumes

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you and your partner planned what the first 6 months look like separately for each of you — not just as a household unit?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the couple has stress-tested the transition at the individual level; vague household-level plans typically mean the trailing partner's situation hasn't been concretely mapped
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If yes: does the trailing partner's plan include a realistic job search timeline and financial bridge for the gap period?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If no: the decision is premature — the trailing partner's first 6 months are the highest-risk period and require explicit planning before committing

diagnostic_questions.question: What would it look like concretely if you remained in the US but maximized your support from here?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the professional has seriously modeled the remote support option or is treating it as obviously inadequate without examination
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If they have modeled it: What specific care need does this option fail to meet, and is that gap large enough to justify the career cost of returning?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If they haven't modeled it: What professional care options exist in the parents' city, and what would high-quality funded care cost relative to the earnings differential of staying?

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you spent significant time with people who returned to your home country 3–5 years ago? What do they say?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Reveals whether the person has calibrated expectations against post-honeymoon-phase returnee experience, or is relying on first-year returnees or no social proof at all
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What is their overall assessment — do they report having stabilized, still struggling, or having re-emigrated? What do they wish they had known?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The person is missing the most relevant data point available — talking to year 3–5 returnees before deciding should be a non-negotiable step

diagnostic_questions.question: Where will your savings be held and in what currency — and have you modeled currency depreciation risk?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person understands that nominally equal savings in local currency may lose real value against USD over a 10–20 year horizon
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Have you looked at the 10-year historical trajectory of that currency against USD, and does your plan depend on converting back to USD at any point?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Review historical RMB or INR depreciation periods against USD before treating local savings as equivalent to USD savings

diagnostic_questions.question: Which specific sector are you in — Tech/AI, Finance (PE/VC vs. state), Academia, Medicine, Law/Government, or Entrepreneurship?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: The baseline return viability, income compression range, and career ceiling risk — these differ so significantly across sectors that the sector answer largely determines the initial prior on return viability
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Within that sector, are you targeting the sub-segment with strong returnee demand (e.g., AI research, PE/VC) or the weaker sub-segment (e.g., state banking, IT services)?
