industry_realities.actual_reality: O-1A removes H-1B cap and lottery constraints, is renewable indefinitely, and directly builds the evidentiary record for EB-1A self-petition — making it a strategic bridge toward the only no-backlog path available to most Indian nationals
industry_realities.implication: For Indian nationals who can qualify for O-1A, it is not merely an H-1B alternative — it is the beginning of a deliberate EB-1A strategy that bypasses the entire per-country backlog system

industry_realities.common_belief: The stay-or-return framework for immigrants applies equally to US H-1B holders and Canadian PR holders
industry_realities.actual_reality: Canadian PR is achievable in 1–2 years vs. a 134-year EB-2 backlog for Indian nationals in the US; the visa precarity driver that dominates US stay-or-return decisions is substantially absent for Canadian PR holders, changing almost every part of the framework
industry_realities.implication: Frameworks written for US H-1B holders should not be applied to Canadian PR holders without significant adjustment; the Canadian decision is structurally less urgent and more flexible

industry_realities.common_belief: Canadian salaries are broadly comparable to US salaries for the same tech roles, so the financial case for Canada vs. returning home is similar to the US case.
industry_realities.actual_reality: Canadian salaries are 25–40% lower than USD equivalents for the same role, and Canadian taxes are higher than most US states — the savings arithmetic is structurally worse in Canada than in the US for the same career level.
industry_realities.implication: Advisors and professionals must use Canada-specific models; applying US frameworks to Canadian situations produces wrong conclusions about whether staying beats returning home

industry_realities.common_belief: US-born children of Chinese parents can freely use their US citizenship in China
industry_realities.actual_reality: China does not recognize dual citizenship and treats US-born children of Chinese nationals as Chinese nationals while they are in China; they may be unable to use their US passport to enter or exit China and will eventually face a forced citizenship choice
industry_realities.implication: Parents must obtain Chinese identity documents for the child, understand local school enrollment policies, and explicitly plan for the eventual citizenship election — not assume US citizenship protects the child in China

industry_realities.common_belief: If my partner is supportive of the return decision, the dual-career problem is resolved.
industry_realities.actual_reality: Stated support and genuine preference alignment are different things. Research documents that at least one partner typically suffers career interruption, status decline, or career relinquishment after international relocation — this happens regardless of initial stated support.
industry_realities.implication: Support must be interrogated: what specifically does the partner want for their own career, and is there a viable path for it in the destination? Emotional support for the decision does not mean career viability in the destination.

industry_realities.common_belief: Professional elder care in China and India is inadequate and cannot substitute for family presence.
industry_realities.actual_reality: High-quality professional elder care — including paid live-in caregivers, care facilities, and care coordination services — is increasingly available and affordable in tier-1 cities in both China and India; a US salary can fund care quality that would be unaffordable on a local salary
industry_realities.implication: Before treating physical return as the only way to meet a care obligation, professionals should explicitly research the cost and quality of professional care in their parents' specific city and model whether funded care is a genuine substitute for the specific need

industry_realities.common_belief: Returning home will feel like relief — familiar language, family, food, and culture will make things easier
industry_realities.actual_reality: The harder part of living abroad is often coming back, not leaving. The person who returns is not the same person who left, and home will feel unfamiliar in ways that are disorienting and hard to explain
industry_realities.implication: Budget emotionally and practically for an adjustment period of 12–24 months, not a smooth re-entry — and don't interpret the difficulty as evidence the decision was wrong

industry_realities.common_belief: A $200K US salary is obviously superior to any home-country equivalent because it's 2–3× higher in gross terms
industry_realities.actual_reality: After federal tax, California state tax, FICA, San Francisco rent, healthcare, and immigration legal fees, $200K in SF may yield only $62K in liquid annual savings — which can be comparable to or lower than a well-compensated home-country role in PPP-adjusted terms
industry_realities.implication: Never compare gross salaries across countries; always run the full deduction model to net liquid savings before drawing conclusions

industry_realities.common_belief: A US MD or JD credential travels internationally and allows you to continue practicing in your home country
industry_realities.actual_reality: Medical and legal licenses are country-specific; a US MD must pass Chinese medical licensing exams in Mandarin to practice clinically in China; a US JD must pass a separate bar qualification to practice Indian or Chinese law — the credential does not transfer
industry_realities.implication: Medical and legal professionals must treat return as a career transition, not a credential transfer — and plan for a multi-year re-qualification process or a pivot to research, teaching, compliance, or entrepreneurship roles

industry_realities.common_belief: Staged return means staying longer in the US — it is about accumulating more time before leaving
industry_realities.actual_reality: Staged return is about defining clear, pre-committed, measurable conditions for return and holding to them — the point is to avoid indefinite delay, not to justify more time in the US
industry_realities.implication: If you are using 'staged return' as a label for an unplanned open-ended stay, you are not doing a staged return — you are defaulting to indefinite stay with a more comfortable name for it

industry_realities.common_belief: A higher US salary means you are better off financially than a returnee
industry_realities.actual_reality: Net savings rate, not gross salary, determines wealth compounding; a person earning $200k in San Francisco and saving $30k/year may accumulate less real wealth than a returnee earning ¥40k/month in Shanghai and saving ¥25k/month while living rent-free near family
industry_realities.implication: Build a full savings-rate model before using salary as a proxy for financial outcome; include taxes, rent, immigration legal fees, remittances, and purchasing power of savings

industry_realities.common_belief: The US pays 3–4x more than home countries, making it financially superior
industry_realities.actual_reality: After purchasing power adjustment, effective taxes, rent, and cost of living, the real savings rate gap is often much smaller — and in some cases, a senior role in a Tier 2 home city generates comparable or higher net savings
industry_realities.implication: Never make stay-vs-return decisions on nominal salary; always model after-tax, after-cost savings rates and project net worth over 10 years

industry_realities.common_belief: The green card process is a temporary waiting period that will resolve in a few years
industry_realities.actual_reality: For Indian nationals on EB-2/EB-3, current backlogs represent 50-100+ year waits under present conditions — it is not a waiting period, it is a structural exclusion for most people in this category
industry_realities.implication: Career plans that are contingent on green card approval for Indian nationals should be restructured entirely around EB-1A, O-1, Canada PR, or return — not around the EB-2/EB-3 queue

industry_realities.common_belief: Staying in Canada is financially comparable to staying in the US for tech professionals
industry_realities.actual_reality: Canadian tech salaries are 25–40% lower than US equivalents in USD terms; the after-tax annual savings differential for comparable roles (e.g., Toronto SWE vs. Seattle SWE) is approximately 3–5× in favor of the US
industry_realities.implication: Tech professionals who frame the decision as 'stay in North America vs. return home' are missing a significant financial variable; the Canada-vs-US decision deserves its own explicit analysis

industry_realities.common_belief: Having Canadian PR means the financial decision has been made — you stay and build from here.
industry_realities.actual_reality: PR eliminates immigration uncertainty but does not change the underlying savings arithmetic — a professional with PR in Vancouver on a single income can still be in a near-zero savings situation that a home-country return would improve
industry_realities.implication: PR should be treated as a valuable benefit that needs to be explicitly priced, not as a decision that forecloses financial analysis

industry_realities.common_belief: OCI status gives Indian-origin children equivalent access to Indian schools and universities
industry_realities.actual_reality: OCI holders are foreign nationals in India; they face a separate NRI/OCI university admission quota with fewer seats, different (often higher) fee structures, and in some sectors require work permits
industry_realities.implication: Parents targeting elite Indian universities like IITs or AIIMS for their OCI-holding children need to research the NRI quota specifically, not assume domestic admission pathways apply

industry_realities.common_belief: A 'take turns' agreement fairly distributes the career sacrifice between partners.
industry_realities.actual_reality: Phase 2 re-emigration is routinely deferred indefinitely in practice. New circumstances (children, elderly parents, new opportunities in the home country) continuously provide reasons to delay, and there is no enforcement mechanism for the sacrificing partner.
industry_realities.implication: A take-turns plan without explicit, binding conditions for Phase 2 is functionally a unilateral sacrifice dressed as a mutual agreement. If Phase 2 conditions cannot be specified concretely, the plan should not be treated as real.

industry_realities.common_belief: The decision about returning for eldercare is primarily about what the parent needs.
industry_realities.actual_reality: In many cases, the return decision is as much or more about the professional's own peace of mind and guilt management as it is about an actual expressed parental need; parents in many cases would prefer the child succeed and visit frequently rather than return and disrupt their career
industry_realities.implication: Professionals should have an explicit conversation with parents about their actual preferences before making a return decision on their behalf — the parent's answer is often different from what the professional assumes

industry_realities.common_belief: Repatriation distress is worst immediately after return
industry_realities.actual_reality: Distress peaks 6–12 months post-return, after the honeymoon phase ends — relationship satisfaction and sense of belonging dip most sharply in months 6–12, not months 1–3
industry_realities.implication: People who feel fine in the first few months and then deteriorate sharply often misread the timeline as 'the decision was wrong' when it is actually the predictable peak of a known adjustment curve

industry_realities.common_belief: PPP adjustment makes home-country salaries comparable to US salaries across the board
industry_realities.actual_reality: PPP applies only to locally produced goods and services; internationally priced items — electronics, imported goods, international schools, international travel — are priced at or near global rates and do not benefit from PPP
industry_realities.implication: Segment your spending into local and international buckets before applying PPP; professionals with internationally oriented lifestyles will find their effective PPP benefit is significantly lower than headline figures suggest

industry_realities.common_belief: China's talent recruitment programs (Thousand Talents, Yangtze River Scholar) are primarily bureaucratic or symbolic
industry_realities.actual_reality: The packages are financially substantive — research startup funds of ¥500K–¥5M, salary supplements, housing subsidies, and lab setup funding are real and actively deployed; Chinese scientific output is now internationally competitive in STEM fields
industry_realities.implication: Academic returnees to China should evaluate these programs seriously as financial and career propositions, not dismiss them — the main constraint is field-specific academic freedom, not program credibility

industry_realities.common_belief: Your US credentials and resume will be recognized and valued by home-country employers without additional relationship-building
industry_realities.actual_reality: Credentials are visible but unverifiable without trusted intermediaries; the home-country employer market is relationship-driven and a strong resume from a FAANG company does not substitute for a warm introduction from someone who knows your work quality
industry_realities.implication: Network credentialing — building 3–5 specific relationships who can hire or refer you — must be treated as a first-order milestone alongside savings and title, not an afterthought

industry_realities.common_belief: Returning home means failing or giving up
industry_realities.actual_reality: A person returning with a top-university degree, 2-3 years of US work experience, English fluency, and an international network has elite credentials and premium positioning in most home markets; the failure framing comes from peer groups who are also afraid, not from realistic outcome assessment
industry_realities.implication: Recalibrate the baseline: the question is not 'am I failing by returning' but 'which path compounds more value for my specific situation over 10 years'

industry_realities.common_belief: Working hard and getting strong reviews will eventually lead to C-suite or VP-level roles in the US
industry_realities.actual_reality: Many senior leadership roles remain harder to access for non-native English speakers or those without deep US cultural roots — this is a structural ceiling, not a skill gap
industry_realities.implication: Assess the leadership composition of your organization and industry before assuming the US ceiling is as high as compensation benchmarks suggest

industry_realities.common_belief: Returning home means starting over and competing as a junior candidate
industry_realities.actual_reality: Returning professionals with US credentials, international experience, and cross-cultural fluency carry a specific returnee premium — they typically enter at senior levels with startup equity opportunities and a structural advantage over domestic-only peers
industry_realities.implication: Return should be evaluated as entering from a position of advantage, not as a retreat — this changes both the timing calculus and the negotiating posture

industry_realities.common_belief: Healthcare is a major reason to stay in Canada, just as it is in the US
industry_realities.actual_reality: Universal healthcare is already included in the Canadian system and does not differentiate 'stay in Canada' from other options for most people; it is an anchor that distinguishes Canada from the US, not Canada from the home country
industry_realities.implication: Healthcare should be removed from the stay-in-Canada argument unless the person has chronic conditions or family members with significant health needs; it is not a universal stay-factor in the Canadian context

industry_realities.common_belief: Canada's universal healthcare means professionals have more take-home pay than their US counterparts, making the financial case for Canada stronger.
industry_realities.actual_reality: While universal healthcare does eliminate premium deductions, it does not offset the combination of lower CAD salaries, higher provincial taxes, and Toronto/Vancouver housing costs relative to comparable US markets — the net effect still favors the US for financial accumulation
industry_realities.implication: Healthcare benefit is real and should be included in models, but it does not change the fundamental conclusion that Canada's savings arithmetic is weaker than the US for the same career level

industry_realities.common_belief: Returning to a lower cost-of-living country will significantly improve the family's savings rate
industry_realities.actual_reality: US-born children are typically excluded from public school systems in China and India, forcing families into international schools that cost $6,000–$50,000 per child per year — an expense that can eliminate or reverse the savings-rate advantage
industry_realities.implication: Any financial model for returning must include per-child international school costs as a line item before the conclusion is valid

industry_realities.common_belief: A spousal or family reunion visa in the destination country resolves the partner's ability to work there.
industry_realities.actual_reality: In China and India, family reunion or spousal visas provide residency rights but work authorization is separate and typically requires employer sponsorship from a local employer. Residency and the right to work are legally distinct.
industry_realities.implication: Couples with a foreign-born partner must separately verify work authorization pathways in the destination country before assuming the partner can continue their career there.

industry_realities.common_belief: The collision of peak career years with eldercare pressure is bad timing that could have been avoided.
industry_realities.actual_reality: The overlap is structural and predictable: parents of typical international students are in their 60s–70s exactly when the student is in their peak career years in their 30s–40s; this is not an exception but the norm
industry_realities.implication: This collision should be anticipated and planned for in advance rather than treated as an unexpected disruption; professionals in their late 20s and early 30s should already be modeling what their response will look like

industry_realities.common_belief: Deep cultural integration abroad is purely an asset with no cost
industry_realities.actual_reality: Genuine cross-cultural formation creates Third Culture Individuals who belong neither fully in the home country nor fully in the host country — belonging everywhere and nowhere is the actual cost of deep integration
industry_realities.implication: For people who integrated deeply, the 'returning home' frame is psychologically misleading — the decision is not between home and abroad but between two places where you partially belong

industry_realities.common_belief: 401k savings are real savings that count toward your financial position
industry_realities.actual_reality: 401k funds are locked until age 59½ (with 10% penalty plus taxes for early withdrawal); for professionals making major life decisions in their 30s and 40s, this capital is not available and should not be treated as equivalent to liquid savings
industry_realities.implication: Maintain two separate mental accounts: liquid annual savings (decision-relevant) and retirement accumulation (long-term); compare scenarios on the liquid number

industry_realities.common_belief: Income compression means the return is financially inferior
industry_realities.actual_reality: Gross income compression (30–85% depending on sector) does not translate proportionally into savings or wealth compression; a physician earning 70% less in China may save 3–4x more annually in PPP-adjusted terms because cost of living differentials are large
industry_realities.implication: Evaluate return economics on net savings rate and PPP-adjusted wealth accumulation, not gross salary comparison — the decision calculus changes significantly when the right metric is used

industry_realities.common_belief: Once you return to your home country, returning to the US is extremely difficult or impossible
industry_realities.actual_reality: Realistic re-entry options include remote work for US companies (normalized post-COVID), US companies expanding into your home country, direct US return within 5–7 years while experience is fresh, and third-country intermediary options (Singapore, Canada, UK)
industry_realities.implication: The mental model of permanence is a cognitive distortion that leads to suboptimal decisions at both ends — either indefinite delay or premature rushed return; frame it as a phase with evaluation conditions instead

industry_realities.common_belief: The immigration decision is binary: get the green card or return home
industry_realities.actual_reality: There are multiple intermediate and alternative paths — EB-1A extraordinary ability self-petition, O-1 visa, L-1 intracompany transfer, Canada PR, Singapore employment pass, Dubai — with different probability profiles, timelines, and opportunity costs
industry_realities.implication: Before accepting the binary, consult an immigration attorney about alternative pathways; the option that dominates may not be on the default menu

industry_realities.common_belief: The green card is a realistic near-term milestone that justifies enduring current visa constraints
industry_realities.actual_reality: For Indian nationals in EB-2/EB-3 categories, wait times are 50–100+ years at current rates — the green card is effectively not a real planning horizon for most
industry_realities.implication: Indian nationals should treat permanent temporary status as the baseline scenario and make career and wealth decisions accordingly, rather than optimizing around a green card that may never arrive

industry_realities.common_belief: The US is where the best opportunities are, and home markets are a step down
industry_realities.actual_reality: The opportunity gap has narrowed structurally in specific high-growth sectors (AI/EV/biotech/fintech in China; VC-backed tech in India), and home markets offer entrepreneurship optionality that the US visa system structurally blocks
industry_realities.implication: Sector-specific opportunity comparison — not a generic US-vs-home assumption — is required; the answer is different for an AI researcher, a fintech operator, and a biotech scientist

industry_realities.common_belief: Canadian PR, once obtained, is effectively permanent and requires no active management
industry_realities.actual_reality: Canadian PR requires 730 days of physical presence in Canada in every rolling 5-year window; extended home-country absences can accumulate to jeopardize PR status, and border officers can make compliance findings on reentry
industry_realities.implication: PR holders who plan extended home-country trips or return-and-visit patterns must actively track their physical presence using Service Canada tools and plan trips to remain compliant

industry_realities.common_belief: A Bangalore or Hyderabad tech professional returning from Canada will be financially worse off because Indian salaries can't match Canadian compensation.
industry_realities.actual_reality: In PPP-adjusted savings terms, a senior Indian tech professional earning ₹50L+ in Bangalore can match or approach the savings of a Toronto dual-income household — the raw salary comparison is misleading without PPP and cost-of-living adjustment
industry_realities.implication: The stay-vs-return financial comparison must be done in PPP-adjusted savings, not gross salary comparison — the home-country option is more financially competitive than it appears in nominal terms

industry_realities.common_belief: Children are resilient and will adapt quickly to a new country and school system
industry_realities.actual_reality: Children in the 8–14 age range are at peak sensitivity for social identity formation and educational track continuity; disruption at this stage carries meaningful risk of the child never fully adapting to either system
industry_realities.implication: The general 'children are resilient' heuristic should not be applied uniformly — the 8–14 window requires a specific, concrete adaptation plan, not optimism

industry_realities.common_belief: A split-family arrangement will self-resolve once the triggering condition (equity vesting, school year end) is met.
industry_realities.actual_reality: Split-family arrangements rarely self-resolve on the planned timeline. 'Temporary' arrangements extend, and research shows relationship quality declines significantly beyond 6 months of split-family living.
industry_realities.implication: Split-family arrangements require a hard decision point at or before 6 months — not a soft target, but an explicit date with defined outcomes for both scenarios (reunite vs. make a permanent decision).

industry_realities.common_belief: Waiting until a health crisis to make a return decision is acceptable because you can respond quickly when needed.
industry_realities.actual_reality: Forced decisions made in the acute phase of a health crisis are reliably worse than planned decisions — career timing is poor, financial preparation is absent, partner situations are unresolved — and produce regret regardless of the direction chosen
industry_realities.implication: The eldercare return decision should be modeled and planned before a crisis, not after one; the practical value of the framework is to create a planned response that can be executed without crisis-state decision-making

industry_realities.common_belief: Returning home is a single transition event
industry_realities.actual_reality: A significant minority of returnees re-emigrate within 2–5 years, often to a third country — making the return decision actually a potential two-transition sequence with compounded disruption
industry_realities.implication: The true cost of returning should be calculated with the realistic probability of a second move factored in, not just the cost of the initial return

industry_realities.common_belief: Immigration fees are a one-time cost that you pay once and forget
industry_realities.actual_reality: H-1B and green card legal and filing fees recur annually over a multi-year process, typically totaling $5K–$15K/year during the green card processing period, which can last 5–15+ years
industry_realities.implication: Model immigration costs as a recurring annual line item in the US scenario for as long as you remain in the green card queue, not as a sunk cost or one-time expense

industry_realities.common_belief: 'China tech' or 'India finance' return opportunity is broadly positive, so a specific role in that sector should be attractive
industry_realities.actual_reality: Within each country and sector, there is a dramatic split between private-market roles (where returnee premium is real) and state-owned or government-affiliated roles (where career ceiling is real and returnee premium is weak) — the sector-level signal does not apply uniformly
industry_realities.implication: Evaluate each specific employer and role type rather than using country-sector aggregate signals; the state/private distinction is the most important sub-classification within any sector

industry_realities.common_belief: The most important milestones before returning are savings and professional title
industry_realities.actual_reality: Network is the most underrated milestone — the person who returns with strong home-country relationships finds a role in 1–3 months; the person without them takes 6–18 months and often ends up back in the US
industry_realities.implication: Deliberate network-building while still in the US — advising, conferences, consulting — should begin 2–3 years before planned return, not after arrival

industry_realities.common_belief: Because most people in your cohort are staying, staying is the right choice
industry_realities.actual_reality: Peer groups self-select around shared decisions; people who returned are systematically underrepresented in your local social network; you are measuring the prevalence of stayers among stayers
industry_realities.implication: Actively seek out returnees from your cohort and talk to them; their experience is data that your current social network is structurally filtering out

industry_realities.common_belief: The H-1B only affects where you can work — your career mobility within that job is unaffected
industry_realities.actual_reality: Research shows 50% of visa-holding researchers felt trapped in their roles and 80% reported restricted job prospects; employer leverage from high switching costs systematically depresses wage growth
industry_realities.implication: Treat visa status as a negotiating constraint that affects salary, career pivots, and entrepreneurial options — not just geography

industry_realities.common_belief: The US compensation advantage makes staying financially superior
industry_realities.actual_reality: The exceptional US compensation figures ($350K-$1M+ at senior levels) represent top performers at elite companies; for mid-level roles at non-elite companies, the advantage is smaller and may not offset immigration restrictions, equity limitations, and psychological costs
industry_realities.implication: Honest assessment of your realistic compensation trajectory — not the headline FAANG figures — is required before concluding that staying is financially optimal

industry_realities.common_belief: Returning to your home country means losing your Canadian PR
industry_realities.actual_reality: Canadian PR holders can live outside Canada for up to 3 consecutive years while maintaining PR as long as they meet the 730-day requirement over the 5-year window; the circular migration path (return home, maintain PR, return to Canada later) is a realistic and structurally supported option
industry_realities.implication: The stay-or-return decision in Canada is not necessarily permanent; PR holders can return home for substantial periods without forfeiting their status if they plan the physical presence compliance carefully

industry_realities.common_belief: Getting a salary increase is the primary way to improve your financial position in Canada.
industry_realities.actual_reality: Ontario and BC marginal tax rates capture 35–45% of each incremental dollar, making salary the weakest lever relative to housing optimization, adding a second income, or childcare subsidy capture
industry_realities.implication: Professionals should rank levers by actual savings impact: dual income first, housing location second, childcare subsidy third, province fourth, salary fifth

industry_realities.common_belief: A return to the home country is primarily a decision about the parents' career and finances
industry_realities.actual_reality: Once children are in the picture, the decision frame expands to include children's identity formation, educational continuity, citizenship status, and long-term optionality — factors that often outweigh the career and financial variables
industry_realities.implication: Parents with children should weight child-specific factors as primary variables in the decision, not secondary considerations to be addressed after the move

industry_realities.common_belief: The stay-or-return decision is binary: stay in the US or return to the home country.
industry_realities.actual_reality: For mixed-nationality couples or couples where one partner faces work authorization barriers in the other's home country, third countries (Singapore, Canada) often provide cleaner immigration and career pathways for both partners simultaneously.
industry_realities.implication: Third-country options should be explicitly evaluated before finalizing a binary choice, particularly for dual-earner couples where at least one partner is not a national of the destination country.

industry_realities.common_belief: Family and friends back home will provide the social support needed for re-adaptation
industry_realities.actual_reality: Friends who stayed have a decade of shared experiences the returnee missed; the enthusiasm of family and friends subsides after the first few months, and the returnee is left with social relationships that feel superficial or misaligned
industry_realities.implication: Social infrastructure for repatriation needs to be actively planned and built — especially through returnee communities — not assumed to exist through existing family and friend networks

industry_realities.common_belief: Home-country real estate is a reliable wealth-building vehicle that improves the financial case for returning
industry_realities.actual_reality: Chinese real estate has been in a significant downturn as of 2023–2025; historical strong performance does not guarantee future returns, and local real estate markets carry country-specific regulatory and economic risks
industry_realities.implication: Do not assume home-country real estate will replicate past performance; model real estate appreciation conservatively and separately from the salary comparison

industry_realities.common_belief: Returning to India for tech means going to TCS, Infosys, or Wipro
industry_realities.actual_reality: IT services firms are explicitly identified as less attractive for returning FAANG engineers; the relevant return market is FAANG India offices, Indian unicorns (Flipkart, Swiggy, Zepto), and AI/ML research roles — which have materially different compensation and career trajectories
industry_realities.implication: India-origin tech professionals should specifically target the unicorn and MNC India office tier, not the IT services tier — the returnee premium does not exist at IT services for someone with senior US tech experience

industry_realities.common_belief: US-trained physicians can return to clinical practice in their home country with the same career and financial trajectory they would have had staying in the US
industry_realities.actual_reality: Income compression from US physician to home-country physician is so severe that many US-trained physicians choose not to return to clinical practice at all; viable return paths are typically research/academic, industry/medtech, or administration
industry_realities.implication: Medicine requires field-specific staged return planning that accounts for licensing complexity and income compression — a generic financial milestone framework does not apply

industry_realities.common_belief: You can always return later if staying does not work out
industry_realities.actual_reality: The return option degrades with time; returning at 25 is categorically different from returning at 40; entrepreneurial windows, family relationship windows, and social capital formation windows narrow each year
industry_realities.implication: Treat the return option as a depreciating asset with a time dimension; evaluate it on the basis of what is available now that will not be available in 10 years

industry_realities.common_belief: US education investment pays off because of the salary premium it unlocks
industry_realities.actual_reality: Total investment including education, living costs, immigration fees, and foregone earnings reaches $400k–$800k before permanent status — this only generates positive ROI at elite outcomes, not median ones
industry_realities.implication: Model your realistic probability of achieving elite outcomes before committing to or continuing the US path; for median outcomes, the case is weaker than students typically model

industry_realities.common_belief: The stay-vs-return decision is a one-time permanent choice
industry_realities.actual_reality: The highest-expected-value path is often staged: stay 3-5 years to hit a specific milestone, accumulate credentials and savings, then return from strength — treating it as reversible and staged rather than permanent
industry_realities.implication: Defining a concrete milestone and timeline converts a paralyzing permanent decision into an actionable near-term plan with a built-in reassessment point

industry_realities.common_belief: Getting Canadian citizenship is just a formality after PR and doesn't need to be strategically timed
industry_realities.actual_reality: Canadian citizenship requires 3 years of physical presence within a 5-year window; for someone considering returning home, delaying to obtain citizenship creates a time cost that may conflict with home-country career or family timelines, while early return forfeits the passport's global mobility value
industry_realities.implication: Citizenship timing should be evaluated as a deliberate strategic decision against the home-country return timeline, not deferred as an assumed eventual step

industry_realities.common_belief: Canada's subsidized childcare ($10/day CWELCC) is a nice benefit but not financially significant in the stay-vs-return calculus.
industry_realities.actual_reality: The difference between subsidized and unsubsidized childcare represents $12,000–$21,600/year — enough to swing a family's savings rate from negative to positive, and one of the highest-impact financial variables in the Canadian model
industry_realities.implication: Childcare subsidy eligibility and availability should be explicitly modeled in any stay-vs-return analysis for families with young children in Canada

industry_realities.common_belief: Dual-earner couples have more flexibility because they have two incomes to buffer the transition.
industry_realities.actual_reality: Research finds that dual-earner couples are materially less geographically mobile than single-earner couples precisely because both careers must survive the transition simultaneously. Two careers create two constraints, not two buffers.
industry_realities.implication: Dual-earner couples should expect harder logistics, longer planning horizons, and more constrained city options than single-earner couples — not easier ones.

industry_realities.common_belief: Reverse culture shock is a sign of weakness, ingratitude, or failure to adapt
industry_realities.actual_reality: Reverse culture shock is a documented psychological and neurological process — the brain's prediction systems are literally recalibrated by extended abroad living, and returning home produces genuine neurological dissonance, not a character flaw
industry_realities.implication: Returnees should be given explicit permission to name and mourn the previous life without shame; suppressing that grief prolongs adjustment

industry_realities.common_belief: The financial comparison between staying and returning will clearly favor one option
industry_realities.actual_reality: After running a complete model, many people find the two scenarios are within 10–20% of each other financially — the model's value is in removing false certainty, not in producing a clear winner
industry_realities.implication: Expect the model to narrow the decision to a range, not resolve it; prepare to make the final call on non-financial variables rather than waiting for the math to decide

industry_realities.common_belief: China's regulatory crackdowns on tech and finance were one-time events and the sector has stabilized
industry_realities.actual_reality: The source identifies finance sector regulatory scrutiny as an ongoing and increased risk since 2021; the Ant Financial IPO cancellation, private tutoring restrictions, and gaming limits represent a pattern of government intervention in private-sector activity
industry_realities.implication: China finance and consumer tech return decisions should include explicit scenario planning for regulatory risk, not just point-in-time compensation benchmarking

industry_realities.common_belief: It is more honest or straightforward to quit your US job before beginning the home-country job search
industry_realities.actual_reality: Resigning before securing a home-country role eliminates your negotiating leverage, removes the US-anchor signal that home-country employers value, and puts you under implicit time pressure that forces acceptance of suboptimal offers
industry_realities.implication: The discomfort of interviewing while employed is real but the cost of the alternative is significantly higher — interview for home-country roles while still employed, accept before giving notice, and negotiate start dates around vesting events

industry_realities.common_belief: Your visa status is just a paperwork inconvenience that does not affect your career
industry_realities.actual_reality: Visa status systematically forecloses opportunities available to domestic peers: founding companies, switching employers freely, taking unpaid career risks, negotiating aggressively; this compounds into a measurable career disadvantage over years
industry_realities.implication: Explicitly inventory the opportunities you have declined or cannot pursue due to visa status; price that cost into the stay decision

industry_realities.common_belief: Home country markets are still far behind the US in career opportunity, especially in tech
industry_realities.actual_reality: China ranks 4th globally for VC investment with competitive AI, EV, and biotech sectors; India ranks 5th for unicorns and has a $1.25B national AI Mission; IIT Madras cohorts going to the US dropped from ~50% to 10–20% — a real opportunity signal
industry_realities.implication: Reassess home country opportunity using current data, not 10-year-old assumptions; the gap has narrowed materially and in some sectors reversed

industry_realities.common_belief: The US vs. home country is the relevant comparison set
industry_realities.actual_reality: Third-country options — Canada (near-certain PR via Express Entry), Singapore (strategic Pan-Asian positioning), UAE (zero income tax), UK (Global Talent Visa) — represent potentially dominant alternatives that are systematically underexplored
industry_realities.implication: The expert's first move is to expand the option set to at least four geographies before evaluating the binary — the best answer may not be either of the two most obvious options

industry_realities.common_belief: Childcare costs in Toronto are prohibitively high and eliminate the savings advantage of Canadian income
industry_realities.actual_reality: Canada's CWELCC program subsidizes childcare costs significantly, reducing market rates from $2,000+/month to $700–$1,000/month for eligible families in Ontario — this subsidy is real and material but still leaves net monthly savings thin at ~$1,400–$1,700 CAD for a typical profile
industry_realities.implication: The childcare subsidy should be factored into financial models but does not eliminate the savings gap; the correct conclusion is that savings are thin, not negative — which is a different and important distinction for the decision

industry_realities.common_belief: Academia is a difficult field for staged return because US tenure-track positions are hard to leave
industry_realities.actual_reality: Academia is the field where staged return is best aligned — home-country universities (through programs like Thousand Talents, Excellent Young Scientists Fund) are specifically recruiting for US research positions, and longer US tenure with more publications directly increases negotiating power for startup funds, salary supplements, and housing packages
industry_realities.implication: Academic professionals should view their US position as an asset that appreciates over time for home-country negotiation purposes — staying longer with continued publication output translates directly into better return offers

industry_realities.common_belief: 'I'll think about stay vs. return after I get my green card' is a reasonable deferral
industry_realities.actual_reality: For many nationalities the green card backlog is 10-50+ years; deferring the decision to that milestone means the decision is made by inertia rather than choice, with roots deepened and options narrowed
industry_realities.implication: Make an explicit conscious decision on the stay-vs-return question now, independent of the green card timeline; do not outsource the decision to bureaucratic timing

industry_realities.common_belief: Returning home means giving up your international career advantage
industry_realities.actual_reality: Returnees (海归) have premium positioning at many home country companies that value international exposure; regulatory and language advantages are scarce and genuinely valuable in growing markets
industry_realities.implication: International credentials can be more competitively differentiating in a home market hungry for that profile than in a US market saturated with similarly credentialed immigrants

industry_realities.common_belief: Most top graduates from elite home-country institutions still move to the US and stay
industry_realities.actual_reality: At IIT Madras, the percentage of undergraduates moving to the US has dropped from roughly 50% to 10-20% over one generation; China's government launched a K-visa in 2025 to compete directly with the H-1B for returning talent
industry_realities.implication: The social proof and peer comparison that made staying the default choice for earlier cohorts no longer applies — the decision is now genuinely bilateral and contested, not a one-way flow

industry_realities.common_belief: Immigration legal fees are a minor administrative cost
industry_realities.actual_reality: Total immigration legal costs over a full green card process run $20,000–$100,000, paid directly from compensation and invisible in salary comparisons
industry_realities.implication: Treat immigration legal costs as a direct reduction to US compensation when building financial models

industry_realities.common_belief: A Canadian job offer adds 200 CRS points
industry_realities.actual_reality: A job offer adds 200 points only for NOC TEER 0 senior manager or NOC 00 roles; most professional job offers (TEER 0/1 excluding NOC 00) add only 50 points
industry_realities.implication: Candidates who believe any job offer adds 200 points will overestimate their CRS and be surprised; the 50-point reality is still significant but requires recalibration of strategy

industry_realities.common_belief: Express Entry is fully meritocratic — if your CRS score is high enough, you'll get invited
industry_realities.actual_reality: CRS score is necessary but not sufficient; draw cutoffs fluctuate based on applicant pool composition and IRCC policy decisions, meaning a 480 score can clear one draw and fail the next draw
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should not treat their CRS score as a guaranteed ticket; they should actively monitor draw trends and have a PNP contingency plan ready

industry_realities.common_belief: Changing jobs while on PGWP is risky for immigration and should be avoided to protect your PR pathway
industry_realities.actual_reality: PGWP is an open work permit — holders can change employers, industries, or job titles freely without any immigration consequence
industry_realities.implication: Career decisions made under this misconception cost the person growth and income for no immigration benefit; PGWP holders should evaluate job changes purely on career merits

industry_realities.common_belief: Students have 90 days after program completion before they need to worry about status or work authorization
industry_realities.actual_reality: The 90-day implied status period allows the student to remain in Canada legally, but work authorization is not automatic during this gap — if the study permit has expired and the PGWP is not yet approved, the student cannot work
industry_realities.implication: Students who line up jobs starting immediately after graduation may find themselves unable to legally work during the PGWP processing gap; employers and students both need to build in this contingency

industry_realities.common_belief: Large Canadian tech companies like Shopify are good targets for PGWP holders because of their Canadian headquarters and familiarity with work permits
industry_realities.actual_reality: Large Canadian tech companies receive flooded application volumes that make cold applications nearly futile; they are not easier to access for PGWP holders than mid-size companies, and may be harder due to volume
industry_realities.implication: PGWP holders should deprioritize large brand-name Canadian employers in their initial job search and focus on mid-size companies where human review and referrals have more impact

industry_realities.common_belief: PGWP holders need employer sponsorship, just like in the US
industry_realities.actual_reality: PGWP is an open work permit — employers take no action, incur no cost, and have no administrative role. The worker holds the permit independently.
industry_realities.implication: PGWP holders should never frame their status as requiring sponsorship; doing so creates a false barrier and disadvantages them in a screening process where no barrier legally exists

industry_realities.common_belief: Consulting and staffing firms are good fallback options for international students who need sponsorship
industry_realities.actual_reality: Consulting and staffing firms often explicitly prohibit sponsorship due to client site restrictions — the client may not allow sponsored workers, making this category one of the least viable for international students needing H-1B
industry_realities.implication: International students should deprioritize or carefully vet consulting and staffing roles early in their job search rather than treating them as safe fallbacks

industry_realities.common_belief: HR and recruiters are the right first contact for cold outreach because they manage hiring
industry_realities.actual_reality: HR and recruiters apply screening criteria — including sponsorship filters — before any personal evaluation; hiring managers, by contrast, are motivated to solve a specific problem and evaluate candidates on fit first
industry_realities.implication: Cold outreach to HR by international students almost always triggers sponsorship filtering before any human judgment; the correct target is the hiring manager or team lead

industry_realities.common_belief: Going to a top-5 CS PhD program is the most important factor for getting into industry research at FAANG or top AI labs
industry_realities.actual_reality: FAANG and top AI labs recruit from a wider range of PhD programs than academic faculty jobs do; the advisor's industry network and internship pipeline matters more than program ranking for industry placement
industry_realities.implication: Students should investigate advisor-level industry connections rather than optimizing solely for program prestige when the goal is industry research

industry_realities.common_belief: A company that verbally commits to H-1B sponsorship during hiring is legally or practically obligated to follow through
industry_realities.actual_reality: Verbal promises of H-1B sponsorship are not legally binding. Companies can and do change internal policy without consequence. Promissory estoppel claims are difficult to prove and expensive to litigate
industry_realities.implication: Employees must treat any offer without written sponsorship language as an offer with no sponsorship commitment, regardless of what was said in the hiring conversation

industry_realities.common_belief: Losing your job or resigning ends your OPT status
industry_realities.actual_reality: Termination or voluntary resignation ends your authorized employment at that employer, but does not immediately end your OPT status — you have up to 90 aggregate days of unemployment before OPT status is affected
industry_realities.implication: Students who panic and assume their status is immediately terminated after job loss may make unnecessary rushed decisions; understanding the buffer allows for more deliberate next steps

industry_realities.common_belief: Because USCIS has never explicitly banned Day 1 CPT, it is a legally safe path to early work authorization
industry_realities.actual_reality: USCIS silence on a practice does not equal endorsement. SEVP has shut down Day 1 CPT schools, consular officers flag them, and USCIS issues RFEs on H-1B petitions citing Day 1 CPT history — the legal risk is real even without an explicit ban
industry_realities.implication: Students must evaluate the enforcement landscape, not just the absence of a formal prohibition; 'not banned' is not the same as 'safe'

industry_realities.common_belief: Cap-exempt H-1B sponsorship is only available at traditional universities and is not relevant for people in industry
industry_realities.actual_reality: Some industry employers have cap-exempt affiliated entities (nonprofit research arms, hospital systems, university partnerships) that can sponsor H-1B outside the cap and outside lottery timing
industry_realities.implication: Workers in industry should proactively ask HR about affiliated cap-exempt entities before assuming the only path is the annual lottery

industry_realities.common_belief: Any employer affiliated with a university is automatically cap-exempt for H-1B purposes
industry_realities.actual_reality: Cap-exempt status requires the entity's primary purpose to be research (or education for universities themselves); for-profit university spinouts, hospitals primarily providing medical care, and grantmaking foundations that don't conduct research themselves do not automatically qualify — even with a university name or affiliation
industry_realities.implication: Candidates and employers should verify the specific entity's qualification before initiating the filing strategy; relying on brand affiliation without legal verification wastes time and creates false security

industry_realities.common_belief: Finance and consulting internship recruiting works on the same timeline as tech — apply in winter or spring for the following summer
industry_realities.actual_reality: Banking summer analyst recruiting can begin in August of junior year — earlier than tech — and positions close before most students realize recruiting has started
industry_realities.implication: Students targeting finance or consulting must research industry-specific timelines (e.g., Wall Street Oasis) and begin even earlier than tech peers

industry_realities.common_belief: The emotional and psychological toll of immigration uncertainty is a personal weakness or overreaction that people should manage privately
industry_realities.actual_reality: Immigration lawyers, mental health professionals, and experienced community members confirm this is a recognized form of chronic stress — corroborated by rank=5 (therapy comment), rank=8 (287 upvotes: 'emotional aspect is real and matters'), and rank=12 (immigration lawyer explicitly validating it)
industry_realities.implication: Seeking therapy, peer support, or community resources is not a sign of weakness — it is appropriate risk management for a legitimately stressful structural situation; withholding this support costs decision quality

industry_realities.common_belief: Winning the H-1B lottery means you can stay in the US
industry_realities.actual_reality: H-1B lottery selection is only the first step; USCIS separately adjudicates whether the specific job qualifies as a specialty occupation requiring a degree that a US worker cannot fill — and denials are common for generic business/non-technical roles at small companies
industry_realities.implication: Do not treat H-1B lottery odds as the only risk to model; assess specialty occupation eligibility and employer petition track record before counting on staying
industry_realities._source: zhihu_出国留学后到底是否回国工作.txt

industry_realities.common_belief: A foreign degree automatically gives returnees a significant advantage in the Chinese job market
industry_realities.actual_reality: For graduates of non-top-ranked institutions, the advantage has largely disappeared — domestic graduates and returnees now compete on near-equal footing, a shift the post says began 'several years ago'
industry_realities.implication: Returnees from non-elite programs must compete on actual skills, cross-border experience, and specific employer fit rather than relying on the credential label
industry_realities._source: zhihu_出国留学后应不应该回国.txt

industry_realities.common_belief: The US stay-or-return decision is primarily a financial optimization problem — compare salaries and cost of living
industry_realities.actual_reality: Financial outcomes in the top cases (FAANG CS) produce unhappiness as often as satisfaction; the dominant predictor of reported life satisfaction in the sample set is social integration and life texture, not income level
industry_realities.implication: People optimizing purely on income are solving the wrong equation; social fit, cultural belonging, and having an engaging life outside work need explicit evaluation
industry_realities._source: zhihu_如果你已经有了美国工作签_你会选择留美还是回国.txt

industry_realities.common_belief: International students choose CS and tech because they love coding and it's a great career
industry_realities.actual_reality: Most Chinese international students in CS chose it because it is one of very few fields where non-citizens can realistically find employment — defense, aerospace, government, and most traditional industries are effectively closed to them
industry_realities.implication: The apparent concentration of Chinese immigrants in CS is a structural artifact of citizenship-based employment restrictions, not revealed preference — many are in careers they didn't truly choose
industry_realities._source: zhihu_未来应留在美国还是回国生活.txt

industry_realities.common_belief: Comparing the raw salary numbers between a US offer and a China offer tells you which country is financially better
industry_realities.actual_reality: Both the best-answer author and the Shanghai returnee explicitly state that the salary numbers are not comparable — $37K USD is a low US salary just as RMB 110K is a low Shanghai salary; the comparison requires local-tier adjustment, not currency conversion
industry_realities.implication: People who stay in the US primarily for the salary premium may be preserving a much smaller actual advantage than they think once cost of living, taxes, and local purchasing power are applied
industry_realities._source: zhihu_海归女硕士一枚_快毕业了是继续留在美国还是回国工作.txt

industry_realities.common_belief: Over 80% of Chinese STEM PhD graduates from US universities stay in the US
industry_realities.actual_reality: This figure was cited approvingly by US Secretary of State Blinken as a policy success — meaning it is a documented retention statistic, not a myth, and is treated by the US government as strategically valuable
industry_realities.implication: The strong retention rate among Chinese STEM PhDs reflects genuine pull factors (career, immigration pathways, innovation ecosystem) rather than mere inertia — but it also means this cohort is explicitly recognized and valued by US national security and innovation policy

industry_realities.common_belief: Returning home with overseas credentials gives you a meaningful competitive advantage in the job market
industry_realities.actual_reality: Many sea-returnees earn only a few thousand RMB per month — the market is saturated with returnees and overseas credentials alone do not translate to premium compensation without local networks and relevant experience
industry_realities.implication: Returnees should assess their value proposition in home country market specifically, not assume overseas experience is automatically valued

industry_realities.common_belief: TEF Canada is harder or equivalent to DELF and requires near-fluency to pass at B1
industry_realities.actual_reality: TEF Canada is widely considered more lenient than DELF; B1 is achievable in 3-6 months of consistent study for English speakers with no prior French background
industry_realities.implication: Candidates who dismiss French as too difficult are leaving up to 50 CRS points unclaimed due to an incorrect difficulty assessment

industry_realities.common_belief: Canadian and US tech salaries are comparable, especially in Toronto
industry_realities.actual_reality: Toronto comp has improved but comparable roles still pay 25-35% less than Bay Area; the poster who chose Canada acknowledged this explicitly even while recommending Canada
industry_realities.implication: Financial modeling for the Canada vs. US decision must account for this delta compounded over 10-20 years, not just current lifestyle cost-of-living adjustments

industry_realities.common_belief: The immigration process anxiety is a personal weakness or failure to cope
industry_realities.actual_reality: The anxiety is a rational response to genuine systemic uncertainty — multiple years of status limbo, CRS score volatility, and policy changes are objectively stressful; the problem is when the anxiety exceeds the actual risk level
industry_realities.implication: Framing anxiety as weakness prevents people from seeking community support or making behavioral changes that would help; reframing it as a normal response to an objectively uncertain system is therapeutically and practically more useful

industry_realities.common_belief: PGWP length exactly matches the length of the degree program completed
industry_realities.actual_reality: PGWP is capped at a maximum of 3 years regardless of program length; a 4-year bachelor's degree does not result in a 4-year PGWP
industry_realities.implication: Students completing 4+ year programs should not assume they receive more than 3 years of post-graduation work authorization; Express Entry and PR planning should account for the 3-year cap

industry_realities.common_belief: A Canadian network is a nice-to-have advantage in job searching
industry_realities.actual_reality: A Canadian local network is a primary job search mechanism — referral response rates (~30%) are roughly 15x cold application response rates (~2%), making networking the dominant activity, not a supplement
industry_realities.implication: Job seekers should treat local meetup attendance and relationship-building as higher-priority activities than submitting applications, especially in the first 60 days

industry_realities.common_belief: Getting into Express Entry is mainly about work experience and education
industry_realities.actual_reality: Language scores — especially the addition of French TEF/TCF — are among the most impactful and controllable CRS levers available to post-graduate applicants, often worth more marginal points than additional work experience
industry_realities.implication: Applicants should treat language test maximization as a core strategy, not an afterthought, and evaluate French investment seriously if any background exists

industry_realities.common_belief: Asking 'will you require sponsorship in the future?' is discriminatory and potentially illegal
industry_realities.actual_reality: This question is legally permitted because it asks about work authorization status, not national origin — employers cannot discriminate based on citizenship status but can legally ask about future sponsorship needs
industry_realities.implication: Candidates who refuse to answer or who push back on the question as discriminatory are misinformed and may create friction unnecessarily — answer honestly

industry_realities.common_belief: Applying through job portals is the primary viable job search channel for new grads
industry_realities.actual_reality: The original poster reported approximately 1% callback rates from job portals over two months, then generated 3 interviews and 1 offer in 6 weeks through cold outreach — corroborated by community response (1243 upvotes)
industry_realities.implication: For international students where sponsorship flags may suppress portal callbacks further, cold direct outreach to managers is a structurally more efficient channel and should be the primary strategy, not a fallback

industry_realities.common_belief: 'Industry research' is a single, well-defined career path that a PhD uniformly prepares you for
industry_realities.actual_reality: Industry research is a spectrum — Applied Scientist at Amazon and Research Scientist at DeepMind are very different roles with different PhD requirements, publication expectations, and daily realities
industry_realities.implication: Students should identify the specific role type they are targeting and evaluate PhD programs against the actual requirements of that specific role, not industry research as a monolithic category

industry_realities.common_belief: L-1 and O-1 visas are accessible backup options when H-1B sponsorship falls through
industry_realities.actual_reality: L-1 requires 1+ year of prior employment abroad with the same multinational employer. O-1 requires genuinely extraordinary ability with significant evidence. Both are narrow and most people in standard software engineering roles do not qualify
industry_realities.implication: These should not be counted as realistic fallback options unless eligibility has been verified with an immigration attorney; planning around them without verification is a failure mode

industry_realities.common_belief: The 60-day grace period gives you time to keep working while finding a new job after H-1B rejection
industry_realities.actual_reality: The 60-day grace period explicitly prohibits work — it is for transitioning status or departing, not continuing employment
industry_realities.implication: Students who work during the grace period believing it is authorized are working without valid work authorization, creating serious immigration violations

industry_realities.common_belief: The H-1B cap-exempt transfer only works if you are already in H-1B status
industry_realities.actual_reality: This is contested in the community — commenter with 76 upvotes raised this as an open question, and the mechanism differs depending on whether you are transferring an existing H-1B vs. obtaining initial cap-exempt sponsorship
industry_realities.implication: Do not assume cap-exempt strategies work the same way for initial H-1B seekers vs. those transferring — consult an immigration attorney for the specific scenario

industry_realities.common_belief: Prevailing wage requirements are different or waived for cap-exempt H-1B petitions
industry_realities.actual_reality: Based on community questioning (145 upvotes on this question with no authoritative rebuttal in the thread), this is an unresolved community uncertainty — the same prevailing wage requirements apply to cap-exempt petitions, but the community frequently assumes otherwise
industry_realities.implication: Candidates should explicitly confirm prevailing wage obligations with their immigration attorney when evaluating a cap-exempt arrangement; do not assume lower salary requirements

industry_realities.common_belief: A strong internship performance is sufficient to secure a return offer; expressing desire to return full-time is unnecessary or even unprofessional
industry_realities.actual_reality: Managers actively advocate for interns they know want to return; interns who do not express interest are frequently passed over in return-offer deliberations even with strong performance reviews
industry_realities.implication: Explicitly communicating intent to return full-time is a material input to the return-offer decision, not a social nicety

industry_realities.common_belief: Job changes for visa holders are normal career decisions with the same flexibility as for citizens or permanent residents
industry_realities.actual_reality: When authorization is employer-specific (H-1B, OPT), leaving a job carries immigration status risk that non-immigrants do not face — confirmed by rank=10 (198 upvotes: 'leaving a job is not simple when your authorization is employer-specific')
industry_realities.implication: Career decisions — accepting offers, leaving toxic environments, negotiating — must be evaluated with immigration status as an explicit variable, not a secondary concern

industry_realities.common_belief: Returning to China as a 海归 (overseas returnee) gives you a significant hiring advantage
industry_realities.actual_reality: The returnee premium has eroded significantly; top domestic Chinese graduates from elite universities compete directly for the same BAT and major company roles, and returnees who cannot adjust salary expectations or who lack relevant domestic experience struggle in the social recruiting market
industry_realities.implication: Do not return to China assuming the overseas credential alone creates a fast track; research your specific target industry and company hiring norms before deciding
industry_realities._source: zhihu_出国留学后到底是否回国工作.txt

industry_realities.common_belief: Finance and business are safe, high-return career paths for international students in the US
industry_realities.actual_reality: Post-2008 financial crisis conditions, reinforced by COVID, have contracted US finance hiring and made the employment environment significantly more difficult; the 'halo' around US finance degrees has faded
industry_realities.implication: Students choosing US finance/business programs primarily for employment upside should stress-test that assumption against current market conditions and factor in the additional barrier of OPT/H-1B sponsorship
industry_realities._source: zhihu_出国留学后应不应该回国.txt

industry_realities.common_belief: Getting H-1B is the main barrier; once you have it, the path to staying is stable
industry_realities.actual_reality: H-1B grants work authorization but not job security; tech layoffs have demonstrated that H-1B holders face forced departure within 60 days of termination, making the stay path fragile throughout the entire period until green card approval
industry_realities.implication: H-1B approval should be treated as the beginning of a precarious multi-year period, not as a resolved immigration problem
industry_realities._source: zhihu_如果你已经有了美国工作签_你会选择留美还是回国.txt

industry_realities.common_belief: Silicon Valley is a meritocracy where hard work and technical skill determine advancement
industry_realities.actual_reality: There is a documented ethnic hierarchy: white/Jewish investors and CEOs at top, white and Indian management in middle, Indian and Chinese engineers at lower-middle tiers — Indian professionals occupy a bridging role that Chinese professionals structurally cannot fill due to English fluency and political navigation skills
industry_realities.implication: Chinese engineers should plan careers with the glass ceiling in mind rather than assuming it doesn't exist or that outperforming technically will break through it
industry_realities._source: zhihu_未来应留在美国还是回国生活.txt

industry_realities.common_belief: The US is significantly safer, cleaner, and higher quality of life in all dimensions
industry_realities.actual_reality: The best-answer author and Shanghai returnee both describe US cities as having visible homelessness, limited nightlife, social isolation, and limited food culture compared to Chinese cities; the quality-of-life advantage is real in some dimensions (air, space, safety in suburbs) but significantly overstated for urban lifestyle preferences
industry_realities.implication: Quality-of-life comparisons should be disaggregated by specific dimension rather than assumed to favor the US wholesale — for someone who values urban vibrancy, dining culture, and social density, major Chinese cities may score higher
industry_realities._source: zhihu_海归女硕士一枚_快毕业了是继续留在美国还是回国工作.txt

industry_realities.common_belief: Home country offers entrepreneurial opportunity to anyone with drive and a good idea
industry_realities.actual_reality: Success in home country business at scale requires background, connections, and capital — not just effort; the commenter explicitly notes that few achieve even mid-tier success despite a large entrepreneurial culture
industry_realities.implication: Returnees motivated by entrepreneurship should audit their actual resource base — network, capital, industry relationships — before treating the home market as an open opportunity

industry_realities.common_belief: Improving English IELTS score is the primary language optimization lever for Express Entry
industry_realities.actual_reality: Past CLB 10, English IELTS improvements yield only ~6 marginal CRS points; French language and spouse language scores offer far greater point gains
industry_realities.implication: Time and money spent on IELTS retakes beyond CLB 10 has very low ROI compared to French study or coaching a spouse through IELTS

industry_realities.common_belief: Getting PR or Canadian work authorization means the job market is open to you equally
industry_realities.actual_reality: A 'Canadian experience' bias exists among some employers who specifically prefer candidates with prior Canadian work history, creating a disadvantage for new PGWP holders regardless of their work permit status
industry_realities.implication: New arrivals should factor in a potential adjustment period with lower-paying or more junior roles to build Canadian experience, and should not assume their international credentials transfer immediately at full market value

industry_realities.common_belief: Federal Express Entry (CEC) is the only path to PR after PGWP
industry_realities.actual_reality: Provincial Nominee Programs (PNPs) offer province-specific streams (e.g., BC Tech Pilot, Ontario Masters Graduate) that can nominate candidates directly, bypassing the federal CRS competition entirely
industry_realities.implication: Candidates with low CRS scores or in eligible provinces should research PNP streams in parallel with federal EE rather than waiting passively for a federal draw

industry_realities.common_belief: STEM OPT extension is essentially the same as visa sponsorship and creates the same burden for employers
industry_realities.actual_reality: STEM OPT extension requires the employer to fill out I-983 forms and be E-Verify enrolled — a much lighter lift than H-1B, which requires a full petition, lottery participation, and attorney fees of $3,000–$8,000
industry_realities.implication: When negotiating with companies that are hesitant about 'sponsorship,' drawing a clear distinction between STEM OPT extension and H-1B can unlock offers that would otherwise be declined

industry_realities.common_belief: Being upfront about visa needs from the start is professional and saves everyone time
industry_realities.actual_reality: Multiple high-upvoted comments (456, 176 upvotes) confirm that opening with sponsorship needs triggers rejection before skills are evaluated; the professional calculation is that establishing value first changes the decision context for the employer
industry_realities.implication: International students should treat visa disclosure as a mid-funnel conversation item, not an upfront filter — this is not deceptive but strategic sequencing of information

industry_realities.common_belief: A PhD is a general career accelerator in tech that improves outcomes across software engineering and research roles alike
industry_realities.actual_reality: The PhD premium is real and significant for research roles but barely exists for pure SWE roles; the 4-5 year opportunity cost in foregone SWE salary (~$150K+/year vs ~$32K stipend) is rarely recovered through a SWE-track PhD
industry_realities.implication: Students targeting SWE roles should enter industry directly; the PhD credential does not materially change SWE compensation or career trajectory at most companies

industry_realities.common_belief: University international offices provide complete and accurate guidance on OPT unemployment rules
industry_realities.actual_reality: Multiple commenters (including one with 156 upvotes) report that their university's international office glossed over or omitted the unemployment rule entirely during OPT orientation
industry_realities.implication: Students cannot rely solely on DSO/international office guidance — independent verification with an immigration attorney or official USCIS sources is necessary for high-stakes decisions

industry_realities.common_belief: Any employment attorney can competently handle H-1B filings
industry_realities.actual_reality: H-1B specialty occupation documentation — including SOC code selection and responding to RFEs — requires immigration-specific expertise; general employment attorneys may file competently on form but miss nuances that determine approval
industry_realities.implication: Workers should advocate for immigration-specialized counsel even if their employer's default attorney is a general employment firm

industry_realities.common_belief: The H-1B lottery is something the company worries about after hiring — the student's job is just to get the offer
industry_realities.actual_reality: Companies are significantly more invested in navigating the H-1B lottery for employees they have already trained; the return-offer path leverages this investment dynamic in the student's favor
industry_realities.implication: The internship is not just a conversion opportunity — it is a trust-building mechanism that changes how hard the employer will fight to retain the employee through the lottery

industry_realities.common_belief: One year of US work experience is a meaningful credential for Chinese social recruiting
industry_realities.actual_reality: Many Chinese companies set a 2-year minimum for social recruiting roles; 1 year of overseas experience at a small company is often treated as near-equivalent to fresh-graduate status, but the candidate has already missed campus recruiting — falling into a gap between both tracks
industry_realities.implication: Non-STEM graduates who stay for 12-month OPT should either (a) have a concrete plan to extend via additional education or (b) return in time to participate in campus recruiting — not assume 1-year experience transitions cleanly into social recruiting
industry_realities._source: zhihu_出国留学后到底是否回国工作.txt

industry_realities.common_belief: Canada's immigration pathway for students is similar in difficulty to the US
industry_realities.actual_reality: Canada's PGWP allows 2–4 year open work permits after graduation without a pre-arranged job offer, and PR eligibility begins after just 1 year of work experience — a substantially more accessible pathway than the US H-1B lottery system
industry_realities.implication: Students who are serious about immigration as an outcome should factor this structural policy difference heavily into country selection, not just program rankings
industry_realities._source: zhihu_出国留学后应不应该回国.txt

industry_realities.common_belief: Non-CS fields cannot lead to stable immigration or good outcomes in the US
industry_realities.actual_reality: Niche stable professions (environmental engineering, specialty law, media/communications) can produce green card pathways and satisfying careers — often with better work-life balance and lower layoff risk than tech
industry_realities.implication: People in non-CS fields should research their specific profession's immigration pathway rather than defaulting to 'I can't stay' or attempting forced pivots to coding
industry_realities._source: zhihu_如果你已经有了美国工作签_你会选择留美还是回国.txt

industry_realities.common_belief: Networking is one of the most important career activities and more of it is better
